title: Science in the kitchen: why food browns, bread rises and onions make us cry

summary.text: Hold a whole onion close to your eyes, and nothing happens. Chop the same onion, and your eyes sting within a minute. A whole onion holds no tear gas. The onion's cells make the gas only after a knife breaks them open. A cut apple turns brown in the same way, when chemicals from broken cells meet the air. Heat makes a second kind of brown, on toast, dosa and the crust of bread. Bread rises because gas forms inside the dough and a stretchy net called gluten holds the gas in. Your child dips apple slices in boiling water and toasts four squares of bread. They also wash a ball of dough to find the gluten.
summary.art: A girl of nine at a kitchen counter holding a whole onion close to her eyes, while beside her a woman chops an onion on a board and wipes her eye with the back of her hand.

intro.hook: A cook can carry a bag of onions all the way home with dry eyes. Then she chops one onion, and tears run down her face. Where was the gas that stings her eyes before she picked up the knife?
intro.text: The gas was not in the onion. The onion made the gas after the knife went in. In this unit you test this with a whole onion, a halved onion and a chopped onion. You stop an apple slice from turning brown with two minutes of heat. Then you use heat to turn bread brown, and find what makes it brown faster. You also wash a ball of wheat dough under water until only a stretchy lump is left. That lump is the reason bread can rise.
intro.art: A woman walking home from a market in Madurai with a cloth bag full of onions, smiling, with dry eyes.

outcomes: I can explain why a cut apple or brinjal turns brown: broken cells, an enzyme and oxygen from the air.
I can name three ways to slow or stop this browning, and say why each one works.
I can explain why toast and dosa turn brown: heat changes the sugars and proteins on a dry surface.
I can explain why idli and boiled rice stay pale: wet food cannot get hotter than boiling water.
I can name three gas makers that raise dough and batter: yeast, baking soda with a sour food, and steam.
I can explain what gluten is, and why wheat dough holds gas while rice flour dough does not.
I can explain why chopping an onion makes eyes water, and give two ways to make fewer tears.
I can plan a fair kitchen test, and say how people found out what makes onions sting.

terms.meaning: The tiny living unit that every plant and animal is built from. A cell is too small to see without a microscope.
terms.example: One thin slice of onion holds many thousands of cells.
terms.art: A thin piece of onion skin under a magnifying circle, showing rows of box-shaped cells like bricks in a wall.

terms.meaning: A chemical made by living cells that speeds up one kind of change. Each enzyme does one job.
terms.example: An enzyme in an apple turns the cut surface brown.
terms.art: A small shape like a pair of hands joining two beads together.

terms.meaning: A gas in the air. We breathe it in, and many chemical changes need it.
terms.example: A cut apple browns in air, because the air holds oxygen.
terms.art: A slice of apple on a plate with small dots of gas drawn drifting onto its cut surface.

terms.meaning: The browning of a cut or bruised fruit or vegetable. An enzyme from the broken cells makes brown colour, using oxygen from the air.
terms.example: A cut brinjal turns brown in a few minutes.
terms.art: Half a brinjal on a board, white at the edges and turning brown in the middle.

terms.meaning: To dip a food in boiling water for a short time and then take it out.
terms.example: Cooks blanch cut vegetables before freezing, so that they keep their colour.
terms.art: A ladle holding slices of vegetable in a pan of boiling water.

terms.meaning: The temperature at which a liquid boils. Water in an open pot boils at about 100 degrees Celsius and gets no hotter.
terms.example: Rice in boiling water stays at about 100 degrees Celsius, however high the flame is.
terms.art: A pot of boiling water on a stove with a thermometer in it showing 100.

terms.meaning: The browning of food by strong heat. On a dry surface hotter than about 140 degrees Celsius, sugars and proteins change into brown substances with new flavours.
terms.example: A dosa turns golden brown on a hot tawa.
terms.art: A golden brown dosa on a black tawa.

terms.meaning: The main kind of heat browning. Sugars react with the building units of proteins and make brown colour and new smells.
terms.example: The brown crust of bread comes from the Maillard reaction.
terms.art: A loaf of bread cut open, with a brown crust and a white inside.

terms.meaning: To heat sugar until it turns brown. Sugar can do this alone, without any protein.
terms.example: Sugar heated in a pan for payasam turns into brown caramel.
terms.art: A small steel pan with melted brown sugar bubbling in it.

terms.meaning: Living beings of one cell each, who belong to the fungi. Yeast eat sugar and give off a gas.
terms.example: Bakers mix yeast into dough to make pav rise.
terms.art: A magnified circle showing many small oval cells, some with a smaller bud growing on the side.

terms.meaning: A gas with no colour and no smell. Yeast give off this gas. Baking soda also makes this gas when it meets a sour food.
terms.example: The bubbles in dhokla batter are carbon dioxide.
terms.art: A bowl of batter with small bubbles rising to the top.

terms.meaning: To be changed by yeast or bacteria as they feed. Fermenting often makes gas or a sour taste.
terms.example: Idli batter ferments overnight and rises in the vessel.
terms.art: A steel vessel of batter that has risen up to the rim, with a plate on top.

terms.meaning: A stretchy substance that forms when wheat flour is wetted and kneaded. It is made of wheat proteins joined into a net.
terms.example: Gluten lets a ball of chapati dough stretch without tearing.
terms.art: Two hands stretching a piece of dough into a thin sheet that does not tear.

terms.meaning: A small organ above each eye that makes tears.
terms.example: When onion gas reaches your eye, the tear gland sends tears to wash it away.
terms.art: A side view of an eye with a small gland drawn above it and drops flowing down over the eye.

explanations.concept: A cell keeps its chemicals in separate parts
explanations.definition: A cell is the tiny living unit that plants and animals are built from. Inside a plant cell, different chemicals are stored in separate parts.
explanations.description: An onion, an apple and a tea leaf are all built from cells. Each cell has a wall around it. Inside the cell are smaller parts, each closed off by a thin skin. One part may store a chemical. Another part may store the enzyme that can change that chemical. An enzyme is a chemical made by cells that speeds up one kind of change. While the cell is whole, the two never meet, so nothing happens. A knife, a grater or a set of teeth breaks the cells open. Then the stored chemicals and the enzymes mix. New substances form within seconds or minutes. This one fact explains three things in this unit. It explains why a cut apple browns and why a chopped onion stings. It also explains why crushed mustard becomes sharp.
examples: A whole apple stays white inside for weeks. A cut apple browns within the hour.
A whole clove of garlic has little smell. A crushed clove smells strong at once.
A bruise on a banana turns brown, because the cells under the peel were crushed.
explanations.art: One large plant cell drawn as a box with two closed bags inside, one bag filled with small dots and the other with small scissor shapes.

explanations.definition: Enzyme browning is the browning of a cut or bruised fruit or vegetable. An enzyme from the broken cells makes brown colour, using oxygen from the air.
explanations.description: The cells of an apple hold colourless chemicals called phenols. They also hold an enzyme called polyphenol oxidase. In a whole cell the two are kept in separate parts. A cut breaks the cells at the surface and mixes them. The enzyme then joins oxygen from the air to the phenols. The changed phenols link into long chains, and the chains are brown. So this browning needs three things together: broken cells, a working enzyme and oxygen. Take away any one, and the slice stays pale. The brown substance is harmless to eat, though the taste changes a little. Apples, bananas, brinjals, potatoes, pears and guavas all brown this way. Oranges and lemons do not. Their juice is sour, and the enzyme works badly in sour juice.
examples: A cut brinjal goes brown within a few minutes.
Grated potato for a cutlet turns pink and then grey-brown in the bowl.
A banana slice in a lunch box is brown by lunch time.
explanations.art: Three drawings of one apple slice in a row, white, then cream with brown edges, then brown all over, with a clock above each.

explanations.concept: How to stop cut fruit browning, and when people want it
explanations.definition: Cut fruit stays pale if the enzyme is destroyed or slowed, or if oxygen is kept away.
explanations.description: Heat destroys the enzyme. Two minutes in boiling water are enough for a thin slice. Cooks call this blanching. Sour juice slows the enzyme, so a squeeze of lemon keeps a fruit chaat pale. Lemon juice also holds vitamin C, which turns the changed phenols back before they can link up. A bowl of water keeps most of the oxygen away, so cooks drop cut brinjal and potato into water. Cold slows every enzyme, so a cut apple browns more slowly in the fridge. Sometimes people want this browning. Tea makers roll fresh tea leaves to break the cells. Then they leave the leaves in the air for up to a few hours. The leaves turn copper brown and become black tea. For green tea, the makers heat the fresh leaves first, in a hot pan or in steam. The heat destroys the enzyme, so the leaves stay green. Black tea and green tea come from the same plant.
examples: Cut potatoes wait in a bowl of water before they are fried for bajji.
Lemon juice is squeezed over sliced banana in a fruit salad.
Tea leaves from one bush in the Nilgiris can become green tea or black tea.
explanations.art: A bowl of water with pale cut brinjal pieces in it, next to a plate with brown cut brinjal pieces left in the air.

explanations.definition: Heat browning is the browning of food by strong heat. Sugars and proteins on a hot, dry surface change into brown substances with new smells and tastes.
explanations.description: This browning has nothing to do with the enzyme in cut fruit. Heat destroys that enzyme. Heat browning is made by the heat. There are two kinds. In the first kind, sugars react with the building units of proteins. This is called the Maillard reaction, after the French chemist Louis-Camille Maillard. He described it in 1912. It makes hundreds of new substances. Some are brown, and many have strong smells. They give toast, dosa, roasted coffee, roasted groundnuts and fried onions their smell. In the second kind, sugar turns brown without any protein. This is called caramelising. Table sugar caramelises at about 160 to 170 degrees Celsius. Both kinds need a temperature well above that of boiling water. The Maillard reaction becomes fast above about 140 degrees Celsius. Milk holds both a sugar and proteins, so foods brushed with milk brown quickly. If the heating goes on too long, the food turns black and bitter. Then it has started to burn.
examples: Milk boiled down for a long time in a wide kadai turns light brown and smells of khoa.
Sugar heated in a pan turns golden and then deep brown.
Onions fried slowly in oil turn brown and sweet.
explanations.art: Four pieces of toast in a row, from white to golden to brown to black.

explanations.definition: Water in an open pot boils at about 100 degrees Celsius and gets no hotter. Food that is wet stays near that temperature, which is too low for heat browning.
explanations.description: Turn the flame up under a pot of boiling water, and the water only boils away faster. Its temperature stays at about 100 degrees Celsius. So rice in boiling water never browns. Idli cooks in steam at about 100 degrees Celsius and stays white. A dosa is made from much the same batter. But the batter is spread thin on a tawa at about 200 degrees Celsius. The water at the bottom boils away in seconds. The dry surface then gets much hotter than 100 degrees Celsius, and it browns. Hot oil works in the same way. Oil for frying is at about 170 to 190 degrees Celsius. The outside of a vada dries and browns in the oil. The inside stays wet and pale. A loaf of bread is brown outside and white inside for the same reason. The crust dries and gets very hot. The inside stays moist and does not pass 100 degrees Celsius.
examples: Idli is white, and a dosa from much the same batter is brown.
A boiled potato is pale, and a fried potato chip is golden.
A wet patch on a slice of bread stays pale on the tawa until it has dried.
explanations.art: A white idli on a plate beside a golden brown dosa, with a steamer behind the idli and a tawa behind the dosa.

explanations.concept: Three ways to make the gas that raises dough
explanations.definition: Dough and batter rise when gas forms inside them. Cooks make the gas with yeast, with baking soda and a sour food, or with steam.
explanations.description: The first gas maker is alive. Yeast are living beings of one cell each, and a teaspoon of dry yeast holds billions of them. In warm, wet dough they wake and feed on sugars. They give off carbon dioxide gas and a little alcohol. This is called fermenting. It takes an hour or more. Wild yeast and bacteria do the same work in idli batter overnight. The second gas maker is a chemical reaction. Baking soda meets a sour food, such as curd or lemon juice. Carbon dioxide forms at once, with no waiting. Dhokla, bhatura and most cakes rise this way. The third gas maker is steam. Water turns to steam at about 100 degrees Celsius. The steam takes up about 1,600 times as much room as the water did. A puri has no yeast and no soda. The water in the dough turns to steam in the hot oil, and the steam blows the puri up. Phulka and popcorn puff in the same way.
examples: Pav and naan are raised by yeast.
Dhokla is raised by baking soda or fruit salt meeting sour curd.
A puri and a grain of popcorn are puffed by steam.
explanations.art: Three foods in a row with a small label under each: a pav with tiny oval yeast cells, a square of dhokla with a spoon of white powder, and a puffed puri with a wisp of steam.

explanations.concept: Gluten: the net that holds the gas
explanations.definition: Gluten is a stretchy substance that forms when wheat flour is wetted and kneaded. It is made of wheat proteins joined into a net.
explanations.description: Making gas is only half of rising. The dough must also hold the gas in. Wheat flour contains two kinds of protein that join together when they are wet. Kneading lines them up and links them into a net. The net stretches like a balloon skin when gas pushes on it. In 1728 the Italian scientist Jacopo Beccari is said to have washed a ball of wheat dough in water. The white starch washed away. A grey, stretchy lump stayed in his hand. That lump was gluten. Rice, ragi, jowar, bajra and maize have proteins too, but they do not form gluten. A dough of rice flour cracks when you stretch it. So a jowar bhakri or an akki rotti is patted flat by hand. It does not puff like a loaf. Idli batter holds its gas in another way. Ground urad dal makes the batter thick and slimy, and the slime traps the bubbles. A few people fall ill when they eat gluten. Their illness is called coeliac disease. For most people gluten is an ordinary food protein.
examples: Chapati dough stretches when you roll it. Rice flour dough for kozhukattai cracks at the edges.
The holes in a slice of bread are the places where gas bubbles were held.
Maida dough is stretchier than atta dough, because bits of bran in atta cut into the net.
explanations.art: A hand holding a small grey stretchy lump over a bowl of milky white water.

explanations.concept: What heat does to risen dough
explanations.definition: Heat makes the gas bubbles in dough grow. Then it sets the dough around them, so the holes stay when the food cools.
explanations.description: Raw risen dough is soft, and it falls flat if you press it. Heat changes that in three steps. First the gas in each bubble spreads out as it warms, and some water turns to steam. So the dough swells further in the first minutes of cooking. Next, at about 60 degrees Celsius, the yeast die. Then the starch and the proteins set firm, in the way an egg sets when it is boiled. The walls of the bubbles become solid. Now the gas can leave and the shape stays. Last, the outside dries and browns. The same steps happen when dhokla or idli is steamed. Only the browning is missing, because steam is not hot enough. If a cook opens the lid too early, the walls have not yet set. The cold air makes the gas shrink, and the cake sinks.
examples: A pav in the oven grows taller in the first few minutes.
Steamed dhokla keeps its holes after it cools.
A cake sinks in the middle if the oven door is opened too soon.
explanations.art: A loaf drawn twice, smaller and pale on the left and taller and brown on the right, with the bubbles inside drawn larger in the second loaf.

explanations.definition: A cut onion gives off a gas that stings the eyes. The onion's cells make this gas in two steps after they are broken, and each step needs an enzyme.
explanations.description: An onion takes sulphur from the soil and builds it into a chemical that the cells store. An enzyme is stored in another part of the same cell. A knife breaks the cells, and the two mix. The first enzyme changes the stored chemical into a new one that does not last. A second enzyme at once turns part of that into a gas. Scientists call the gas the lachrymatory factor, which means the tear maker. It forms within about half a minute of the cut. The gas floats up and reaches the wet surface of the eye. Nerve endings there sense it and send a signal to the brain. The brain signals the tear glands, and tears pour out to wash the gas away. Three things make fewer tears. A cold onion makes gas more slowly, because cold slows enzymes. A sharp knife breaks fewer cells than a blunt one. Moving air carries the gas away from the face. A cooked onion cannot sting, because heat destroys both enzymes. Garlic lacks the second enzyme. So crushed garlic makes a strong smell and no tear gas.
examples: Onions chopped straight from the fridge sting less than onions from the basket.
A whole onion boiled in sambar can be cut afterwards with dry eyes.
Crushed mustard seeds mixed with water turn sharp after ten minutes, in a similar way.
explanations.art: A chopped onion on a board with thin wavy lines rising from it towards a person's eye, and a tear running down the cheek.

explanations.concept: Do the sting and the brown protect the plant?
explanations.definition: Most plant scientists think the onion's gas is a defence against animals who would eat the bulb. They disagree about whether browning protects a wounded fruit or leaf.
explanations.description: An onion bulb is alive. They are a resting plant, and they can sprout again. The tear gas is made only when the bulb is bitten or cut. So most scientists see the gas as the onion's defence. The browning of a wound is harder to explain. The brown substances can harm microbes and insects in a dish in the laboratory. Whether they protect a living plant is still being tested.
examples: An onion left in the basket for weeks pushes out a green shoot.
Many animals leave onion bulbs alone.

perspectives.who: Scientists who see a defence, such as Li Li and John Steffens at Cornell University in 2002
perspectives.explanation: They changed tomato plants so that the plants made much more of the browning enzyme. Far fewer harmful bacteria grew in the leaves of these plants. So the enzyme can help a plant resist disease.

Apple trees whose browning enzyme has been switched off still grow and fruit. The enzyme may do other jobs in the cell that nobody has found yet. One result in tomato does not prove what the enzyme does in every plant.

explanations.art: An onion bulb in the soil with a green shoot, and a small beetle turning away from a bite mark on the bulb.

agreed.text: A cut fruit browns because an enzyme from its broken cells joins oxygen to chemicals in the juice.
agreed.evidence: Heat destroys enzymes, and a slice dipped in boiling water does not brown. In 2015 the United States approved apples whose browning enzyme had been switched off. Their slices stay pale for days.

agreed.text: Heat browning comes from sugars reacting with the building units of proteins.
agreed.evidence: In 1912 Louis-Camille Maillard warmed sugars with these building units, which are called amino acids. The clear mixtures turned brown and gave off gas.

agreed.text: Wet food stays near 100 degrees Celsius, so it does not brown.
agreed.evidence: A thermometer in an open pot of boiling water reads about 100 degrees Celsius however high the flame is. Steamed and boiled foods stay pale in every kitchen.

agreed.text: The onion makes tear gas only after cutting, and needs two enzymes to do so.
agreed.evidence: In 2002 Shinsuke Imai and his team in Japan found the second enzyme. Onion juice without this enzyme made almost no tear gas.

agreed.text: Wheat dough holds gas because of gluten.
agreed.evidence: In 1728 Jacopo Beccari is said to have washed wheat dough and been left with a stretchy lump of gluten. Flours that leave no such lump make flat breads.

agreed.text: Yeast are alive, and they make the gas in bread dough as they feed.
agreed.evidence: In the 1850s Louis Pasteur watched yeast under a microscope. He showed that fermenting happens only where living yeast are growing.

challenging.claim: A cut apple that has turned brown has gone bad.
challenging.for: Rotten fruit is often brown, and a brown slice looks less fresh.
challenging.against: The brown comes from the apple's own enzyme within minutes. Microbes need days to rot a fruit. A browned slice is safe to eat.

challenging.claim: Food turns brown on the tawa because it is burning.
challenging.for: Food left too long on the heat does go from brown to black.
challenging.against: Browning comes first and makes new flavours. Burning comes later, when the food breaks down to black carbon and tastes bitter. Golden brown food is not burnt.

challenging.claim: Onion gas turns into acid on the eye, and the acid makes us cry.
challenging.for: The gas does break down in water, and one of the products is an acid.
challenging.against: The amount of gas is very small. Nerve endings on the eye have sensors that react to stinging chemicals themselves. Many scientists now think these sensors respond to the gas directly.

challenging.claim: Holding a piece of bread in your mouth stops onion tears.
challenging.who: A kitchen tip passed on in many families.
challenging.for: Some cooks say it works for them. Breathing through the mouth may draw the gas away from the eyes.
challenging.against: The gas reaches the eyes through the air, and bread cannot catch it. No careful test has shown that the tip works.

challenging.for: People with coeliac disease become ill from gluten. They must avoid wheat for life.
challenging.against: Coeliac disease affects about 1 person in 100. For most people gluten is an ordinary protein, and wheat has been eaten for thousands of years.

challenging.claim: Very brown fried food can harm us.
challenging.who: Margareta Törnqvist and her team in Sweden, in 2002.
challenging.for: They found a chemical called acrylamide in starchy foods fried or baked until dark. In large doses it causes cancer in rats and mice.
challenging.against: People eat far smaller doses than the test animals received. Studies of people have not shown clear harm. Many food agencies still advise cooking to golden and not to dark brown.

big_questions.q: A whole onion holds no tear gas. So is the sting a part of the onion, or something the onion does?
big_questions.hint: Think about the Onion Sting activity. The whole onion did nothing to your eyes, and the chopped onion stung.

big_questions.q: Toast and a cut apple are both brown. What would you test to find out if two browns are the same change?
big_questions.hint: Heat stops one kind of browning and causes the other.

big_questions.q: A dosa and an idli come from much the same batter. Is a food decided by what goes in or by what is done to it?
big_questions.hint: The batter is the same. The temperature at the surface is different.

big_questions.q: The onion makes a stinging gas when cut, and people cut onions every day. Who has won, the onion or the cook?
big_questions.hint: People plant onions on millions of farms because we like their taste.

big_questions.q: Humans are the only animals who cook. How might browned, cooked food have changed our ancestors?
big_questions.hint: Cooked food is softer and gives more energy for less chewing.

big_questions.q: People made bread and black tea for thousands of years before anyone knew about enzymes or yeast. Did they understand what they were doing?
big_questions.hint: A baker knew that dough must be kept warm. Is knowing how the same as knowing why?

story.title: The Handful That Stayed Green
story.note: Malar, Chellamma, Kathir, the shed and the letter are made up. These facts are real. Tea grows around Kotagiri in the Nilgiri hills of Tamil Nadu. Black tea and green tea come from the same plant. For black tea the leaf is wilted and then rolled to break the cells. It is left in the air for up to a few hours to turn brown, and then dried. For green tea the fresh leaf is heated first, in a hot pan or in steam. Then it stays green when rolled. The browning is done by an enzyme in the leaf, the same kind that browns a cut apple.
text: Every evening in the picking season, Malar's hands smelled of cut grass. Her job was to roll the tea.

Her aunt Chellamma made tea by hand in a tin shed above Kotagiri, in the Nilgiri hills. Four families brought their leaf to her. Malar was nine, and she had rolled leaf beside her aunt for two seasons.

The work never changed. In the morning the pickers brought baskets of fresh leaf. Chellamma spread the leaf on cloth racks until it went limp. In the afternoon Malar and her cousin Kathir rolled it. They pressed a heap of limp leaves under their palms and pushed it round and round on a bamboo tray. The leaves twisted and bruised, and green juice wet their hands. Then the rolled leaf lay on trays in the cool end of the shed. In two hours it turned from green to the colour of a new copper pot. Last, Chellamma dried it in a wide iron pan over the wood fire.
That was black tea. It was the only tea the shed had ever made.
On Tuesday a letter came from a shop in Coimbatore. The shop would pay double for green tea. It wanted one kilo by Saturday, to try.
"We cannot do it," said Kathir. He was twelve, and he read the labels on the packets in the bazaar. "Green tea comes from a green tea bush. Ours are black tea bushes."
"Who told you that?" asked Chellamma.
"Everybody knows it."

Chellamma did not answer. She had picked tea since she was a girl, and she had only ever seen one kind of bush. But she had only ever made one kind of tea. She did not know how the other kind was made, and nobody on the hill made it.
Malar said nothing either. She was thinking about last Thursday.

Last Thursday she had carried a basket of fresh leaf past the fire. Her foot had caught on a root that grew across the floor. A handful of leaves had tipped into the hot iron pan. She had snatched them out with the wooden paddle before her aunt could turn round. They were limp and hot, and they smelled like boiled beans. She had been ashamed. She had pushed them into the middle of her heap and rolled them with the rest.

Two hours later she had seen them again. The tray was copper brown from edge to edge. But in the middle lay a few twists of leaf as green as when they were picked. She had picked them out and thrown them to the hens, so that nobody would ask.
Now she went to the cool end of the shed and looked at today's trays. Every leaf was turning brown.
"Chitti," she said. That was what she called her aunt. "Why does the leaf go brown?"
"Because we roll it. Unrolled leaf only dries up. It stays dull green, like hay."
"So the rolling does it."
"The rolling starts it. Then the air does the rest."
"Last week some leaves fell in the hot pan," said Malar. Her ears were burning. "Only for a moment. I rolled them with the others. They never went brown. I threw them to the hens."
Kathir laughed. "You cooked them. Of course they were spoilt."

"They were not spoilt. They were green. They were rolled, and they lay in the air, and they stayed green." Malar turned to her aunt. "Something in the leaf turns it brown after rolling. The hot pan stopped that from working. If we heat the leaf first, and roll it afterwards, it might stay green."
Chellamma looked at her for some time. Then she put two handfuls of fresh leaf into the iron pan.

She stirred with the paddle while Malar counted aloud. The leaves hissed and went soft. At two hundred, Chellamma lifted them out. Malar rolled them on a clean tray. Beside them she rolled two handfuls that had not touched the pan. They put the two trays side by side at the cool end of the shed.
Nobody did much work for the next two hours.
Malar looked after half an hour. The plain leaf had brown edges. The heated leaf was green.
After an hour the plain leaf was brown all over. The heated leaf was green.

After two hours Chellamma came and stood between the trays. She picked up a twist of the green leaf and smelled it. Then she dried both lots in the pan, one after the other, and made two tumblers of tea.
One tea was red-brown and smelled of malt, as their tea always did. The other was pale gold, and it smelled like the hillside after rain.
"Same bush," said Chellamma. She held out the pale tumbler to Kathir. "Drink."
Kathir drank. He looked into the tumbler for a while.
"Everybody was wrong, then," he said.
"Everybody had not dropped the leaf in the pan," said Chellamma.
By Saturday there was a kilo of green tea in a steel tin, tied in a cloth. Malar carried it down to the bus herself. She stepped carefully over the root.
story.epiphany: Kathir was sure that green tea needs a different bush. Malar had seen that leaves heated in the pan stayed green after rolling. Rolling breaks the cells of the leaf, and an enzyme then turns the leaf brown in the air. Heat destroys the enzyme, so leaf that is heated first stays green.
ask: Rolled tea leaves turn brown in the air. What does rolling do to the cells of a leaf?
The heated leaves were rolled too, and they lay in the same air. Why did they stay green?
How could you stop a cut apple from browning, using the same idea?

games.title: Which Change Is It? The kitchen cards
games.context: This is a card game about four kitchen changes. Each card describes something that happens in a kitchen. You say which of the four changes it is, and why.
