printables.title: 20 kitchen cards: what happens on the front, the change and the reason on the back

items.f: A sliced banana in a lunch box is brown by lunch time.
items.b: Enzyme browning. Cutting broke the cells, and an enzyme used oxygen from the air.

items.f: A dosa turns golden on a hot tawa.
items.b: Heat browning. The dry surface gets far hotter than boiling water.

items.f: A puri blows up into a ball in hot oil.
items.b: Gas rise. Water in the dough turns to steam, and the steam fills the puri.

items.f: The cook's eyes water as she chops for the sambar.
items.b: Cut sting. Broken onion cells make a gas that stings the eyes.

items.f: Grated potato in a bowl turns pink and then grey-brown.
items.b: Enzyme browning. Grating breaks a great many cells.

items.f: Sugar in a pan melts and turns deep brown.
items.b: Heat browning. Sugar caramelises at about 160 to 170 degrees Celsius.

items.f: Pav dough left in a warm place doubles in size in an hour.
items.b: Gas rise. Yeast feed on sugar and give off carbon dioxide. Gluten holds the gas.

items.f: Crushed mustard mixed with water becomes sharp in ten minutes.
items.b: Cut sting. An enzyme from the broken seed cells makes the sharp substance.

items.f: A bruise on a guava turns brown under the skin.
items.b: Enzyme browning. The knock crushed the cells, though the skin was not cut.

items.f: The crust of a loaf is brown and the inside is white.
items.b: Heat browning. The crust dried and got hot. The inside stayed wet and below 100 degrees Celsius.

items.f: Dhokla batter froths up when fruit salt is stirred in.
items.b: Gas rise. Baking soda meets a sour food and makes carbon dioxide at once.

items.f: A crushed clove of garlic smells far stronger than a whole one.
items.b: Cut sting. Crushing mixes a stored chemical with an enzyme, and a strong new substance forms.

items.f: Rolled tea leaves turn copper brown on a tray.
items.b: Enzyme browning. Rolling breaks the cells of the leaf, and the air does the rest.

items.f: Onions fried slowly in oil turn brown and sweet.
items.b: Heat browning. Heat has destroyed the onion's enzymes, and the sugars and proteins brown.

items.f: Idli batter rises to the rim of the vessel overnight.
items.b: Gas rise. Wild yeast and bacteria ferment the batter and make gas.

items.f: A cut brinjal goes brown before the oil is hot.
items.b: Enzyme browning. Cooks drop cut brinjal into water to keep the oxygen away.

items.f: Milk boiled down in a kadai turns light brown.
items.b: Heat browning. Milk holds a sugar and proteins, and they react as the milk thickens.

items.f: A grain of maize bursts into popcorn.
items.b: Gas rise. Water inside the grain turns to steam and bursts the hard shell.

items.f: A blunt knife makes more onion tears than a sharp one.
items.b: Cut sting. A blunt knife crushes more cells, so more gas is made.

items.f: A phulka puffs up over the flame.
items.b: Gas rise. Steam forms between the two layers and pushes them apart.

printables.title: 4 change tokens: Enzyme browning, Heat browning, Gas rise, Cut sting. Print one set for each player

rules: One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud. The reader keeps the back hidden.
Every other player puts one change token face down. Then everyone turns the tokens over together.
The reader reads the back. Every player whose token matches the change on the back scores 1 point.
A player who also says why scores 1 more point. The reader decides, using the back of the card.
With two players, swap the reader's role after every card. The reader does not guess on their own card.
Playing alone? Read a card, say the change aloud, then turn the card over. Score 1 point for each right change.
After all 20 cards, the player with the most points wins. If you play alone, your score out of 20 is your result.

flow.do: Cut out the 20 cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile. Give each player one set of four tokens.
flow.say: Each card tells of something that happens in a kitchen. Your four tokens are four kinds of change. Enzyme browning happens to cut fruit. Heat browning happens on a hot, dry surface. Gas rise makes food swell. Cut sting is a sharp gas or taste made by broken cells.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards. Take four tokens.
flow.context: This is the first step of Which Change Is It. You set up the cards and the tokens.

flow.do: Play the first ten cards. After each card, read the back aloud. Ask the question below after card five.
flow.say: The reader reads the front. Choose a token and put it face down. Now turn it over. The reader reads the back. Who scored?
flow.kid: Listen to the card. Pick a change token. Turn it over. Check the back.

ask.q: How did you tell enzyme browning from heat browning?
good: I asked whether the food was heated.
Cut fruit browns in the cold. Toast needs a hot tawa.
Enzyme browning needs broken cells and air.

flow.parent: For a stuck child, ask two things. Was the food cut or crushed? Was it heated on a dry surface? One child can play alone or with you.
flow.context: In this step of Which Change Is It you play the first ten kitchen cards.

flow.do: Play the last ten cards the same way. Keep the score on a piece of paper.
flow.say: Ten more cards. This time, also try to say why. A good reason earns one more point.
flow.kid: Play ten more cards. Say the reason for each change.
flow.context: In this step of Which Change Is It you play the last ten cards and give reasons.

flow.do: Count the points. Then sort all 20 cards into four heaps, one for each change.
flow.say: Let us sort the cards into four heaps. Look at the enzyme browning heap and the cut sting heap. What did every food in those two heaps have done to it?
flow.kid: Sort the cards into four heaps. What is the same in two heaps?

check.q: What starts both enzyme browning and the onion's sting?
check.why: Cutting, grating or crushing breaks cells and mixes chemicals that were stored apart. If you chose heating, remember that heat stops both of these changes. Yeast make gas and have no part in browning or stinging.

flow.context: This is the last step of Which Change Is It. You sort the kitchen cards into four heaps.

games.title: Puff or Flop: the rising game
games.context: This is a dice game about rising. A dough rises only as far as the gas it makes and the gas it can hold. In each round you roll for both, and you keep the smaller number.

setup.art: A die, a bowl of about 60 beans, a pile of twelve face-down cards and a score sheet on a table.
setup.caption: 1. Put about 60 beans in a bowl. Shuffle the 12 kitchen cards into a pile.

setup.art: A child rolling a die, with a notebook showing two columns headed Gas and Hold.
setup.caption: 2. Roll once for Gas and once for Hold. Then turn over a kitchen card.

setup.art: A child's hand taking three beans from the bowl, with the notebook showing Gas 5 and Hold 3.
setup.caption: 3. Take beans equal to the smaller number. That is how far your dough rose.

printables.title: 12 kitchen cards: what happened on the front, the reason on the back

items.f: You kneaded the wheat dough for ten minutes. Add 2 to Hold.
items.b: Kneading links the wheat proteins into a stronger net of gluten.

items.f: You used rice flour alone. Hold becomes 1.
items.b: Rice flour forms no gluten, so the gas escapes.

items.f: The kitchen is cold. Take 2 from Gas.
items.b: Yeast work slowly in the cold and make less gas.

items.f: You mixed the yeast with warm water. Add 2 to Gas.
items.b: Yeast feed fastest when they are warm, at about 30 to 35 degrees Celsius.

items.f: Boiling water was poured on the yeast. Gas becomes 0.
items.b: Yeast die at about 60 degrees Celsius. Dead yeast make no gas.

items.f: You gave the yeast a spoon of sugar. Add 1 to Gas.
items.b: Yeast feed on sugar and give off carbon dioxide.

items.f: The batter stood for an hour after the soda went in. Take 3 from Gas.
items.b: Soda makes its gas at once. The bubbles float out if the batter waits.

items.f: Urad dal was ground well into the batter. Add 2 to Hold.
items.b: Ground urad dal makes the batter thick and slimy, and the slime traps bubbles.

items.f: The cooker lid was opened too early. Take 2 from Hold.
items.b: The walls of the bubbles had not set, so the cake sank.

items.f: The oil for the puri was very hot. Add 2 to Gas.
items.b: Water in the dough turns to steam fast in very hot oil.

items.f: There is a hole in the puri. Hold becomes 1.
items.b: The steam escapes through the hole, so the puri stays flat.

items.f: The packet of yeast was two years old. Take 3 from Gas.
items.b: Most of the yeast in an old packet have died.

printables.title: Score sheet: six rounds for each player

rules: Each round is one bake. On your turn, roll the die and write the number under Gas. Roll again and write the number under Hold.
Turn over the top kitchen card and read the front aloud. Change Gas or Hold as the card says. A number cannot go below 0.
Read the back of the card aloud. It gives the reason.
Look at your two numbers. Take beans equal to the smaller one. If Gas is 5 and Hold is 3, take 3 beans.
Put the card at the bottom of the pile. Then the next player has a turn.
Play six rounds each. The player with the most beans wins.
Playing alone? Play six rounds and count your beans. A total of 18 or more is a very good bake.

flow.do: Put the beans in a bowl. Shuffle the 12 kitchen cards. Give each player a row on the score sheet. Read the rules aloud.
flow.say: A dough needs two things to rise. It must make gas, and it must hold the gas in. In this game you roll the die for each. Your rise is the smaller of the two numbers.
flow.kid: Put beans in a bowl. Shuffle the cards. Listen to the rules.
flow.context: This is the first step of Puff or Flop. You set up the beans, the die and the kitchen cards.

flow.do: Play three rounds each. After each turn, ask the player to say which number held the dough back.
flow.say: Roll for Gas. Roll for Hold. Turn a card and change your numbers. Which number is smaller? Take that many beans. Was it the gas or the hold that kept your dough down?
flow.kid: Roll for Gas. Roll for Hold. Turn a card. Take the smaller number of beans.

ask.q: Your Gas was 6 and your Hold was 2. Why did you get only 2 beans?
good: The dough could hold only 2.
The rest of the gas escaped.
Making more gas does not help if the dough cannot hold it.

flow.parent: The rule of the smaller number is the point of the game. Let your child find it by playing. One child can play alone against the target of 18 beans.
flow.context: In this step of Puff or Flop you play the first three rounds and take beans for each bake.

flow.do: Play three more rounds each. Add up the beans.
flow.say: Three more bakes. Before you turn each card, say which number you hope it will change, and why.
flow.kid: Play three more rounds. Say which number you want the card to change.
flow.context: In this step of Puff or Flop you play the last three rounds and add up your beans.

flow.do: Count the beans. Then ask the check question.
flow.say: Count your beans. Now think about a real kitchen. A baker adds extra yeast to a dough made of rice flour alone. Will the loaf rise higher?
flow.kid: Count your beans. Does more yeast help rice flour dough?

check.q: A dough has Gas 6 and Hold 1. Which change gives a higher rise?
check.why: The rise is the smaller number, which is Hold. Raising Hold from 1 to 3 gives 3 beans. If you chose more gas, remember that the dough cannot hold the gas it already has.

flow.context: This is the last step of Puff or Flop. You count your beans and think about a real dough.

experiments.title: Hot Dip, Cold Dip: can heat stop a cut apple turning brown?
experiments.question: Three slices are cut from one apple. One gets no dip. One is dipped in cold water for two minutes. One is dipped in boiling water for two minutes. Which slices will turn brown in the next 40 minutes?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which of the three slices will be brownest after 40 minutes, and which will be palest? Will the boiled slice brown faster or slower than the others? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Cut all three slices from the same apple, each about half a centimetre thick. Dip the cold slice and the hot slice for the same time, two minutes. Then both have been wet, and only the heat differs. Lay all three slices on one plate in the same place. Look at them at the same times. Only one thing changes: no dip, a cold dip or a hot dip.

materials.item: apple (or a banana, a brinjal or a potato)
a knife, for the grown-up
a small pan of boiling water, and a ladle with holes or a large spoon
a bowl of cold tap water
a steel plate, and three scraps of paper marked N, C and H
a fork
a clock, a notebook page and a pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts the apple and does the dip in boiling water. The child stays an arm's length from the stove.
experiments.record: Draw a table with three rows: no dip, cold dip and hot dip. At each time, write a brown score from 0 to 3. Write 0 for no brown, 1 for a little, 2 for brown patches and 3 for brown all over.
experiments.context: In this experiment you dip one apple slice in cold water and one in boiling water. Then you watch for 40 minutes to see which slices turn brown.

setup.art: Three thin slices of apple on a steel plate, each beside a scrap of paper marked N, C or H.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up cuts three slices, each about half a centimetre thick.

setup.art: A grown-up holding a ladle with an apple slice in a small pan of boiling water, and a second slice sitting in a bowl of cold water.
setup.caption: 2. One slice goes in cold water for two minutes. A grown-up holds one in boiling water for two minutes.

setup.art: Three slices on a plate beside a clock, with the first slice brown, the second light brown and the third pale.
setup.caption: 3. Look at 10, 20 and 40 minutes. Give each slice a brown score.

setup.art: A child's hand drawing a fork across an apple slice, leaving four scratch lines.
setup.caption: 4. At 20 minutes, scratch the no-dip slice and the hot-dip slice with a fork. Watch the scratches.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: brown score from 0 to 3

flow.do: Put the apple, the bowl of cold water and the plate on the table. Ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: We will cut three slices from this apple. One gets no dip. One sits in cold water for two minutes. One sits in boiling water for two minutes. Which will be brownest after 40 minutes? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Three slices: no dip, cold dip, hot dip. Which will go brownest? Why?

ask.q: What do you think heat will do to the slice?
good: It will cook it, so it may go brown faster.
It may kill something in the apple.
I am not sure, but hot things often go brown.

flow.parent: Many children expect the heated slice to brown most, because cooking often browns food. Do not correct the guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of Hot Dip, Cold Dip. You guess which apple slice will turn brown, before you test.

flow.do: Bring a small pan of water to the boil. Cut three slices, each about half a centimetre thick. Put slice N on the plate. Put slice C in the cold water. Hold slice H under the boiling water in the ladle. After two minutes, lift out C and H and put them on the plate. Note the time.
flow.say: I will cut the slices and do the hot dip. You time two minutes on the clock. Both dipped slices get wet. Why did we give one slice a cold dip?
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts and dips. You time two minutes. Then note the time.
flow.parent: The cold dip is the fair partner of the hot dip. Without it, nobody could tell whether the heat or the wetting made the difference. The boiled slice will look a little glassy and soft.
flow.context: In this step of Hot Dip, Cold Dip a grown-up dips apple slices in cold water and in boiling water.

flow.do: Look at the plate after 10 minutes and after 20 minutes. Your child writes a brown score from 0 to 3 for each slice. At 20 minutes they scratch slice N and slice H with a fork, four lines each.
flow.say: Give each slice a brown score from 0 to 3. Now scratch the no-dip slice and the hot-dip slice with the fork. The scratches break fresh cells. What do you think the scratches will look like in 20 minutes?
flow.kid: Score each slice from 0 to 3. Scratch two slices with a fork.

check.q: In Hot Dip, Cold Dip, why do all three slices come from one apple?
options: So that only the dip is different
So that less apple is wasted
So that the slices taste the same
check.why: Two apples may brown at different speeds. Slices from one apple start the same, so any difference comes from the dip. If you chose waste or taste, remember that a fair test changes only one thing.

flow.parent: You can do something else between the looks. The times need not be exact, but look at all three slices together.
flow.context: In this step of Hot Dip, Cold Dip you score the three apple slices and scratch two with a fork.

flow.do: Look again 40 minutes after the dip. Write the last scores. Look closely at the scratch lines on slice N and slice H.
flow.say: Write the last scores. Now look at the scratches. On which slice did the scratch lines turn brown?
flow.kid: Write the last scores. Which scratches turned brown?
flow.context: In this step of Hot Dip, Cold Dip you look at the apple slices and scratches after 40 minutes.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened. The hot slice and the cold slice were both wet. What did the boiling water do that the cold water did not?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: The scratches on the boiled slice stayed pale, though fresh cells were broken. What does that tell you?
good: Whatever makes the brown was destroyed by the heat.
Breaking cells is not enough. Something in the cells must still work.
The boiled slice cannot make brown any more.

ask.q: Name three things that this browning needs.
good: Broken cells.
Something in the apple that still works, the enzyme.
Air, or the oxygen in it.

flow.parent: In most kitchens the no-dip slice is clearly brown by 40 minutes. The cold-dip slice is nearly as brown. The hot-dip slice stays pale, and so do its scratches. Write down what you really saw, even if it differs. The reason: apple cells hold an enzyme and some colourless chemicals in separate parts. Cutting mixes them, and the enzyme joins oxygen from the air to the chemicals. That makes the brown. Boiling water destroys the enzyme. Some apples brown slowly. If your no-dip slice is still pale after 40 minutes, repeat the test with a banana or a brinjal.
flow.think: Tea makers heat fresh leaves in a hot pan to make green tea. What does the heat stop?
flow.context: This is the last step of Hot Dip, Cold Dip. You say what the brown scores of the three apple slices show.

experiments.title: The Tawa Toast Test: which bread square browns most?
experiments.question: Four squares of bread go on one tawa. One is dry, one is wet with water, one with sugar water and one with milk. Which square will be brownest after four minutes?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Put the four squares in order, from the one that will brown least to the one that will brown most. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Cut all four squares from one slice of bread. Put the same amount of liquid, half a teaspoon, on each wet square. Lay all four squares at the same distance from the middle of the tawa. Every minute, move each square one place round the tawa. Then no square sits on a hotter spot for the whole time. Only one thing changes: what is on the bread.

materials.item: slice of white bread
small cups or katoris, for water, sugar water and milk
sugar, 1 teaspoon
milk, 2 tablespoons
a teaspoon, and a half-teaspoon measure if you have one
a tawa, a stove and a pair of tongs
a clock, a notebook page and a pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up works at the stove and handles the tawa and the tongs. The child stands an arm's length away and looks at each square when the grown-up holds it out.
experiments.record: Draw a table with four rows: dry, water, sugar water and milk. After each minute, write a brown score from 0 to 4. Write 0 for white, 1 for cream and 2 for golden. Write 3 for brown like the crust of the bread, and 4 for dark brown.
experiments.context: In this experiment you wet three squares of bread with water, sugar water and milk, and leave one dry. A grown-up toasts all four on a tawa, and you see which one browns most.

setup.art: One slice of white bread cut into four squares on a plate, beside three small cups labelled water, sugar water and milk.
setup.caption: 1. Cut one slice into four squares. Stir 1 teaspoon of sugar into 2 tablespoons of water.

setup.art: A child's finger spreading liquid from a teaspoon over one face of a square of bread.
setup.caption: 2. Spread half a teaspoon of liquid on one face of three squares. Leave one square dry.

setup.art: Four squares of bread on a black tawa, placed like the four petals of a flower around the middle.
setup.caption: 3. A grown-up lays the squares wet side down, at the same distance from the middle.

setup.art: A grown-up holding up one square with tongs to show its brown underside to a child with a notebook.
setup.caption: 4. Each minute, the grown-up shows you each square. Write a brown score.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: brown score from 0 to 4

flow.do: Cut one slice of bread into four squares. Put out the three cups. Ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: One square stays dry. One gets water, one gets sugar water and one gets milk. Then all four go on the tawa. Put them in order, from least brown to most brown. Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Four squares: dry, water, sugar water, milk. Which will brown most? Why?

ask.q: Will the wet squares brown faster or slower than the dry one? Why?
good: Slower, because the water has to dry first.
Faster, because sugar burns easily.
Milk goes brown when it boils over, so milk may brown fast.

flow.parent: Any order with a reason is a good start. Do not correct the guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Tawa Toast Test. You guess which square of bread will brown most, before you test.

flow.do: Stir 1 teaspoon of sugar into 2 tablespoons of water until it dissolves. Your child spreads half a teaspoon of each liquid on one face of a square. Leave the fourth square dry. Write down which square is which.
flow.say: Spread the liquid over the whole face with the back of the spoon. Every wet square gets the same amount. Why must the amount be the same?
flow.kid: Spread half a teaspoon on each wet square. Leave one square dry.
flow.parent: Nip one corner off the water square and two corners off the sugar square. Nip three off the milk square. Then you can tell them apart on the tawa.
flow.context: In this step of the Tawa Toast Test you wet three squares of bread with water, sugar water and milk.

flow.do: Heat the tawa on a low flame for one minute. Lay the four squares wet side down, each halfway between the middle and the edge. After each minute, lift each square with tongs and show the underside. Your child writes the scores. Put each square back one place further round. Stop after four minutes, or sooner if a square turns dark brown.
flow.say: I will lift each square after every minute. Give each one a brown score from 0 to 4. I am moving each square one place round the tawa. Why am I doing that?
flow.kid: Watch from an arm's length away. Score each square every minute.

check.q: In the Tawa Toast Test, why does each square move one place round every minute?
options: Some parts of the tawa are hotter
So that the squares do not stick
check.why: The flame heats some parts of a tawa more than others. Moving the squares round shares the hot spots among them. If you chose sticking or cooling, think about what must stay the same in a fair test.

flow.parent: Keep the flame low. The sugar square can go from brown to black quickly, so take it off if it starts to smoke. Listen for the hiss from the wet squares in the first minute.
flow.context: In this step of the Tawa Toast Test a grown-up toasts the four bread squares. You score them each minute.

flow.do: Turn off the stove. Lay the four squares in a row, toasted side up. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened. Compare the water square with the dry square. Then compare the water square with the sugar square and the milk square.
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: The water square stayed pale for the first two minutes. What was the heat doing in that time?
good: Drying the water.
The water was boiling away.
The bread could not get hot until the water was gone.

ask.q: The water, sugar and milk squares were all wet. Why did two of them end up browner?
good: Sugar browns in heat.
Milk has sugar and protein in it.
They had more of what browning needs.

flow.parent: Usually the dry square browns first. The water square stays pale longest and ends palest. The sugar and milk squares start late and then turn the darkest. Write down what you really saw, even if it differs. The reason: wet bread stays at about 100 degrees Celsius until the water has boiled away. Heat browning needs a dry surface well above that. Browning is a reaction of sugars with proteins. Sugar water adds sugar. Milk adds both a sugar and proteins. So those squares brown most once they have dried.
flow.think: Bakers brush milk on buns before baking. What does the milk do?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Tawa Toast Test. You say what the brown scores of the four bread squares show.

experiments.title: Wash the Dough: what is left of wheat dough and rice dough?
experiments.question: A ball of wheat dough and a ball of rice dough are each washed in a bowl of water. What will be left in your hand from each ball?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. When you wash each ball of dough in water, what will be left in your hand? Will the two flours leave the same thing? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same amount of each flour, half a cup. Knead both balls for the same time, five minutes. Rest both under water for the same time, 15 minutes. Wash each ball in the same way, squeezing gently under water. Change the water each time it turns white. Only one thing changes: the kind of flour.

materials.item: wheat flour, half a cup (maida works best, and atta also works)
rice flour, half a cup
water, about 3 tablespoons for each dough, and more for washing
large bowls or vessels
a tea strainer or a sieve
a clock, a notebook page and a pencil

experiments.safety: Do not taste the raw dough. Pour the white washing water onto plants or down the sink with plenty of water.
experiments.record: Draw a table with two rows: wheat and rice. Write how far each dough stretched before it broke. Write what was left after washing, and how big it was.
experiments.context: In this experiment you make one ball of wheat dough and one ball of rice dough. You wash each ball in water and find out what is left.

setup.art: Two balls of dough on a plate, one cream-coloured and smooth and one white with cracks.
setup.caption: 1. Knead half a cup of each flour with about 3 tablespoons of water for five minutes.

setup.art: Two bowls of water with a ball of dough resting at the bottom of each, beside a clock.
setup.caption: 2. Rest both balls under water for 15 minutes.

setup.art: A child's hands squeezing a ball of dough under milky white water in a large bowl.
setup.caption: 3. Squeeze the wheat ball gently under water. Change the water when it turns white.

setup.art: A child's fingers stretching a small grey lump into a thin sheet over a bowl of nearly clear water.
setup.caption: 4. Keep washing until the water stays nearly clear. Stretch what is left.

flow.do: Put the two flours on the table. Ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: We will make a ball of wheat dough and a ball of rice dough. Then we will wash each ball in a bowl of water. What will be left in your hand from each one? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: You will wash two balls of dough. What will be left? Why?

ask.q: What do you think flour is made of?
good: White powder that mixes into water.
Starch.
I think all of it will wash away.

flow.parent: Most children expect both balls to wash away completely. Do not correct the guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of Wash the Dough. You guess what will be left when wheat dough and rice dough are washed.

flow.do: Mix half a cup of wheat flour with about 3 tablespoons of water. Your child kneads it for five minutes into a smooth ball. Do the same with the rice flour. Pull each ball slowly apart and see how far it stretches. Write that down.
flow.say: Knead by pressing, folding and turning the dough. Count five minutes on the clock. Now pull each ball slowly apart. How far does each one stretch before it breaks?
flow.kid: Knead each dough for five minutes. Pull each ball slowly. Which one stretches?
flow.parent: Add water a teaspoon at a time until the dough holds together. Rice flour may need a little more. The rice ball will crack when it is pulled.
flow.context: In this step of Wash the Dough you knead a ball of wheat dough and a ball of rice dough. Then you stretch each one.

flow.do: Put each ball in its own bowl and cover it with water. Leave both for 15 minutes.
flow.say: Both balls rest under water for 15 minutes. The rest makes the wheat ball easier to wash.
flow.kid: Put each ball in a bowl of water. Wait 15 minutes.
flow.wait: Leave the balls under water for 15 minutes
flow.context: In this step of Wash the Dough the two balls of dough rest under water for 15 minutes.

flow.do: Your child squeezes and kneads the wheat ball gently under the water. When the water turns white, pour it away through the strainer. Put any bits from the strainer back on the ball. Add fresh water. Repeat until the water stays nearly clear, about five or six times. Then wash the rice ball in the same way.
flow.say: Squeeze the ball gently under the water. Look at the water. What is coming out of the dough? Keep the ball in one piece. Now do the same with the rice ball.
flow.kid: Squeeze the wheat ball under water. Change the white water. Then wash the rice ball.

check.q: In Wash the Dough, the washing water turned white. What was the white substance?
check.why: Starch is a fine white powder that floats away in the water. Gluten is the stretchy lump that stays behind. If you chose gluten, remember that gluten does not wash away.

flow.parent: Be gentle at first, or the wheat ball breaks into shreds. The shreds join again if you press them together. With atta, the lump is smaller and has brown specks of bran. The rice ball falls apart into white water, and nothing stays in the hand.
flow.context: In this step of Wash the Dough you wash each ball of dough until the water stays clear.

flow.do: Your child stretches the lump that is left, pokes it and lets it spring back. Ask them to say what they thought would happen, what they found, and why they think it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Stretch the lump. Poke it. Say what you thought would happen, what you found, and why you think it happened. Which dough could hold a bubble of gas without tearing?
flow.kid: Stretch the lump. Say what you thought would happen. Say what you found. Say why.

ask.q: Bread is made from wheat far more often than from rice. Why?
good: Wheat dough has the stretchy part that holds gas.
Rice dough cannot stretch, so the gas escapes.
The lump can stretch like a balloon.

ask.q: The wheat dough stretched and the rice dough cracked. What explains that now?
good: The stretchy lump was inside the wheat dough all along.
Rice flour has no gluten.

flow.parent: Half a cup of maida leaves a grey, rubbery lump about as big as an amla. The lump is gluten. It forms when two kinds of wheat protein join into a net as the dough is wetted and kneaded. The white that washed away was starch. Rice flour has starch and protein too, but its proteins do not form this net. So nothing is left. Gas pushes into the gluten net and stretches it, and that is how wheat dough rises. The Italian scientist Jacopo Beccari is credited with first describing gluten, in a talk of 1728.
flow.think: Idli batter is made of rice and urad dal, with no wheat. What might hold the gas in idli batter?
flow.context: This is the last step of Wash the Dough. You say what was left of the wheat dough and the rice dough.

activities.title: The Onion Sting: whole, halved and chopped

materials.item: onion, of any common kind, kept at room temperature
a knife and a chopping board, for the grown-up
a clock that shows seconds

schedule.what: Hold a whole onion, then a halved onion, near your eyes. Then count the seconds until your eyes sting while a grown-up chops.

activities.safety: A grown-up does all the cutting. The child keeps their face about 30 centimetres from the board, which is the length of a ruler. The sting is harmless and passes in a minute or two. Move away, blink, and do not rub your eyes with oniony fingers.
activities.record: Write three lines: whole onion, halved onion and chopped onion. For each, write whether your eyes stung, and after how many seconds.
activities.context: In this activity you hold a whole onion and then a halved onion near your eyes. Then a grown-up chops the onion while you count the seconds until your eyes sting.

setup.art: A child holding a whole, unpeeled onion about a hand's width from her open eyes.
setup.caption: 1. Hold a whole onion near your eyes for 30 seconds.

setup.art: A child holding half an onion, cut side towards her face, about a hand's width from her eyes.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up cuts the onion in half. Hold one half near your eyes for 30 seconds.

setup.art: A grown-up chopping half an onion on a board while a child watches from a ruler's length away, with a clock on the counter.
setup.caption: 3. A grown-up chops the other half. Count the seconds until your eyes sting.

flow.do: Give your child a whole, unpeeled onion. Ask the question below first, and write down the guess and the reason. Then they hold the onion about 10 centimetres from their open eyes for 30 seconds.
flow.say: Cooks cry when they chop onions. Will this whole onion make your eyes sting from close by? Why do you think so? Now hold the onion near your eyes for 30 seconds.
flow.kid: Will a whole onion sting your eyes? Why? Hold the onion close for 30 seconds.

ask.q: Where do you think the stinging gas is right now?
good: Inside the onion.
Under the skin.
Maybe there is none yet.

flow.parent: A whole onion does not sting and has little smell. Many children expect the gas to be stored inside. Do not correct the guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Onion Sting. You guess whether a whole onion will sting your eyes, and then you test it.

flow.do: Peel and halve the onion. Your child holds one half, cut side towards the face, 10 centimetres from the eyes for 30 seconds. Then chop the other half finely for one minute. Your child watches from 30 centimetres away and counts aloud until their eyes first sting.
flow.say: I have cut the onion in half. Hold one half near your eyes for 30 seconds. What do you feel? Now I will chop the other half. Count the seconds aloud until your eyes sting.
flow.kid: Hold the half onion close. Then watch the chopping. Count until your eyes sting.
flow.parent: The single cut usually gives a faint sting or none. The chopping usually stings within 10 to 40 seconds. If your child does not want stinging eyes, you can be the one who is tested.
flow.context: In this step of the Onion Sting you test a halved onion. Then you count the seconds while a grown-up chops.

flow.do: Move away from the board. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what happened, and why they think it happened.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what happened, and why you think it happened. The whole onion did nothing. The chopped onion stung. Where did the gas come from?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what happened. Say why.

ask.q: Chopping stung far more than one cut. What is different about chopping?
good: It makes many more cuts.
More of the onion is broken open.
More cells are cut.

flow.parent: A whole onion holds no tear gas. Each cell stores a chemical in one part and an enzyme in another. A knife breaks the cells and the two mix. Within about half a minute they make a gas, and the gas floats up to the eyes. More cuts break more cells, so chopping makes far more gas than one cut.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Onion Sting. You say why a chopped onion stung your eyes and a whole onion did not.

activities.title: Two Katori Dhoklas: with soda and without

materials.item: rava (sooji), 6 tablespoons
sour curd, 4 tablespoons
water, 3 tablespoons
salt, 2 pinches
fruit salt, a quarter teaspoon (or a pinch of baking soda with half a teaspoon of lemon juice)
small steel katoris, lightly oiled
an idli cooker, or a kadai with a lid and a small stand
a toothpick and a ruler

schedule.what: Make one batter and split it in two. Add fruit salt to one half. Steam both, and compare the heights and the holes.

activities.safety: A grown-up works at the stove and lifts the hot katoris out of the steam. Wait five minutes before you touch the katoris.
activities.record: Write the height of the batter in each katori before steaming, and the height of each dhokla afterwards. Draw the cut face of each dhokla, with its holes.
activities.context: In this activity you make one rava batter and split it into two katoris. Only one half gets fruit salt. A grown-up steams both, and you compare how far each one rose.

setup.art: A bowl of pale batter being poured into two small steel katoris, each about half full.
setup.caption: 1. Mix the batter and rest it for 10 minutes. Split it into two equal halves.

setup.art: A spoon stirring white powder into one of two small bowls of batter, with froth rising in that bowl.
setup.caption: 2. Stir a quarter teaspoon of fruit salt into one half. Pour each half into a katori at once.

setup.art: Two katoris on a stand inside a kadai of steaming water, and a grown-up placing the lid.
setup.caption: 3. A grown-up steams both katoris for 12 minutes.

setup.art: Two small dhoklas cut in half on a plate, one tall and full of holes and one low and dense, with a ruler beside them.
setup.caption: 4. Measure both. Cut each in half and look at the holes.

flow.do: Mix 6 tablespoons of rava, 4 tablespoons of sour curd, 3 tablespoons of water and 2 pinches of salt. Rest the batter for 10 minutes. Meanwhile, ask the question below and write down the guess and the reason.
flow.say: We will split this batter in two. One half gets fruit salt, and the other gets nothing. Then both are steamed. How will the two dhoklas differ? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Mix the batter. One half gets fruit salt. How will the two differ? Why?

ask.q: What do you think the fruit salt will do in the batter?
good: It will fizz.
It will make bubbles.
It will make the dhokla soft.

flow.parent: Put 2 centimetres of water in the cooker or kadai and bring it to the boil while the batter rests. The batter should drop slowly from a spoon. Add a spoon of water if it is stiffer.
flow.context: This is the first step of Two Katori Dhoklas. You mix a rava batter and guess what fruit salt will do.

flow.do: Split the batter into two small bowls. Your child stirs a quarter teaspoon of fruit salt into one bowl only. Pour each half into a katori at once. Your child dips a toothpick to the bottom of each and measures the wet part.
flow.say: Stir the fruit salt in quickly. What do you see and hear? Now measure how deep the batter is in each katori.
flow.kid: Stir fruit salt into one half. Watch it. Measure both batters with a toothpick.
flow.parent: Fruit salt is baking soda mixed with a dry sour powder. It froths as soon as it is wet. The batter must go into the steam within a minute, before the bubbles escape. Each katori should be about half full.
flow.context: In this step of Two Katori Dhoklas you stir fruit salt into one half of the batter. Then you measure both halves.

flow.do: Put both katoris in the steam and close the lid. Steam for 12 minutes on a medium flame. Lift the katoris out and wait five minutes.
flow.say: Both katoris get the same steam for the same time. I will lift them out when the 12 minutes are over.
flow.kid: A grown-up steams both katoris for 12 minutes. Then wait five minutes.
flow.parent: Do not open the lid in the first 10 minutes. A toothpick pushed into the middle should come out clean.
flow.context: In this step of Two Katori Dhoklas a grown-up steams both katoris for 12 minutes.

flow.do: Your child measures the height of each dhokla with the toothpick. Cut each one in half. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they found, and why they think it happened.
flow.say: Measure both. Now look at the cut faces. Say what you thought would happen, what you found, and why you think it happened. What made the holes?
flow.kid: Measure both. Look at the holes. Say what you guessed, what you found, and why.

ask.q: The holes stayed after the dhokla cooled. Why did the dhokla not sink back?
good: The heat set the batter around the bubbles.
The batter turned solid while the bubbles were still there.

flow.parent: The dhokla with fruit salt usually rises to nearly twice its height and is full of small holes. The plain one stays low and dense. The baking soda met the sour curd and made carbon dioxide gas. The gas made bubbles, and the steam's heat set the batter around them. Both dhoklas are good to eat with chutney.
flow.context: This is the last step of Two Katori Dhoklas. You measure the two dhoklas and look at the holes inside.

activities.title: Wake the Mustard: raw seeds and roasted seeds

materials.item: mustard seeds (rai or kadugu), 2 teaspoons
a mortar and pestle, or a rolling pin and a folded sheet of paper
small katoris
cold water, 2 teaspoons
a small pan with a lid, and a stove

schedule.what: Crush raw mustard seeds and roasted mustard seeds, wet both, wait ten minutes and compare the smell.

activities.safety: A grown-up roasts the seeds, with a lid on the pan, because the seeds jump. Smell each paste from a hand's width away. A sharp paste can sting the nose. Wash your hands before you touch your eyes.
activities.record: Write three lines: dry crushed seeds, raw paste after 10 minutes and roasted paste after 10 minutes. For each, write how sharp the smell was: none, a little or strong.
activities.context: In this activity you crush raw mustard seeds and roasted mustard seeds, and wet both with cold water. After ten minutes you compare how sharp each paste smells.

setup.art: A grown-up holding a lid over a small pan in which mustard seeds are popping.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up roasts 1 teaspoon of mustard seeds under a lid until the popping slows.

setup.art: A child crushing dark seeds with a pestle in a small stone mortar.
setup.caption: 2. Crush 1 teaspoon of raw seeds to a powder. Smell it. Then crush the roasted seeds.

setup.art: Two small katoris of dark paste side by side, one labelled raw and one labelled roasted, beside a clock.
setup.caption: 3. Stir 1 teaspoon of cold water into each powder. Wait 10 minutes. Smell each one.

flow.do: Roast 1 teaspoon of mustard seeds in a dry pan under a lid, on a low flame. Stop when the popping slows, after about one minute. Let them cool. Meanwhile your child crushes 1 teaspoon of raw seeds to a coarse powder and smells it at once.
flow.say: Crush the raw seeds to a powder. Smell the powder from a hand's width away. How sharp is it? I am roasting the other spoonful of seeds.
flow.kid: Crush the raw seeds. Smell the powder. A grown-up roasts the other seeds.
flow.parent: Dry crushed mustard smells only faintly. With no mortar, fold the seeds in a sheet of paper and roll a rolling pin over them hard.
flow.context: This is the first step of Wake the Mustard. You crush raw mustard seeds and smell the dry powder.

flow.do: Your child crushes the cooled roasted seeds in the same way. Put each powder in its own katori. Stir 1 teaspoon of cold water into each. Ask the question below and write down the guess and the reason. Note the time.
flow.say: Both powders now have cold water in them. We will wait 10 minutes. Which paste will smell sharper, the raw one or the roasted one? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Wet both powders. Which will smell sharper in 10 minutes? Why?
flow.context: In this step of Wake the Mustard you wet the raw powder and the roasted powder. You guess which will turn sharp.

flow.do: After 10 minutes, your child smells each paste from a hand's width away, raw paste last. Ask them to say what they thought would happen, what they found, and why they think it happened.
flow.say: Smell the roasted paste first, and then the raw paste. Say what you thought would happen, what you found, and why you think it happened. Think about the apple slice dipped in boiling water in Hot Dip, Cold Dip. That slice could not turn brown.
flow.kid: Smell both pastes. Say what you guessed, what you found, and why.

ask.q: The dry raw powder was mild, and the wet raw paste was sharp. What did the water allow?
good: It let the things in the seed mix and react.
The enzyme needs water to work.

ask.q: Why did the roasted paste stay mild?
good: Heat destroyed the enzyme.
It is like the boiled apple slice, which could not brown.

flow.parent: The raw paste usually turns sharp enough to tingle the nose. The roasted paste stays mild and nutty. A mustard seed stores a chemical and an enzyme in separate cells. Crushing and wetting bring them together, and the enzyme makes the sharp substance. Roasting destroys the enzyme. That is why mustard popped in hot oil for a tadka tastes nutty and not sharp. Cooks in Bengal grind raw mustard with cold water to make a sharp paste for fish.
flow.context: This is the last step of Wake the Mustard. You compare the smell of the raw mustard paste and the roasted mustard paste.

projects.title: Who Turns Brown? A three-day kitchen survey

materials.item: small pieces of the fruits and vegetables your family cuts each day, at least 3 kinds a day
a plate, kept in the same place each day
a clock, a notebook page and a pencil

projects.safety: A grown-up does the cutting. Use only pieces from food that is being cut for a meal, so that nothing is wasted.

schedule.what: Test three or more cut foods from today's cooking. Score each at the start and after 30 minutes.
Test three or more different foods in the same way.
Test the last foods. Then sort all the foods into browners and non-browners and look for a pattern.

projects.record: Make a table with four columns. Write the food, the brown score at the start and the brown score after 30 minutes. In the last column, write whether the food tastes sour. Score from 0 to 3, as in Hot Dip, Cold Dip.
projects.context: In this three-day project you test the fruits and vegetables that your family cuts for meals. You find out which ones turn brown in 30 minutes, and what the browners have in common.

setup.art: A plate with small cut pieces of banana, potato, tomato and carrot, each beside a paper label.
setup.caption: 1. Ask for a small cut piece of each food. Put the pieces on one plate.

setup.art: A child looking at the plate beside a clock and writing numbers in a notebook table.
setup.caption: 2. Score each piece at the start and after 30 minutes.

setup.art: A notebook page with two lists headed Turns brown and Stays the same.
setup.caption: 3. On day 3, sort all the foods into two lists. Look for a pattern.

flow.do: Day 1. When food is being cut for a meal, ask for a thumb-sized piece of three or more kinds. Ask for the guess and the reason first. Your child puts the pieces on a plate and scores each from 0 to 3. They score again after 30 minutes.
flow.say: In Hot Dip, Cold Dip the plain apple slice turned brown in the air. Which of today's foods will turn brown in 30 minutes? Why do you think so? Score each piece now, and again in 30 minutes.
flow.kid: Which cut foods will go brown? Why? Score each piece now and in 30 minutes.
flow.parent: Good foods to try are banana, apple, potato, brinjal, raw banana, guava and pear. Also try tomato, carrot, cucumber, orange, lemon, onion and beetroot.
flow.context: This is day 1 of Who Turns Brown. You test three or more cut foods from today's cooking.

flow.do: Day 2. Test three or more different foods in the same way, on the same plate in the same place. Your child also writes whether each food tastes sour.
flow.say: Today we test new foods. Score each piece now and after 30 minutes. Also write whether each food tastes sour.
flow.kid: Test new foods today. Score them twice. Which ones taste sour?
flow.wait: Do this on the second day
flow.context: This is day 2 of Who Turns Brown. You test more cut foods and note which ones taste sour.

flow.do: Day 3. Test the last foods. Then your child writes all the foods in two lists: turns brown, and stays the same. Ask them to say what they thought would happen, what they found, and what pattern they see.
flow.say: Write two lists. Say what you thought would happen, what you found, and what pattern you see. Look at the sour foods. Which list are they in?
flow.kid: Make two lists. Say what you guessed and what you found. Find a pattern.
flow.wait: Do this on the third day

ask.q: No sour food turned brown. How could a cook use that?
good: Squeeze lemon juice on cut fruit.
Sour juice slows the enzyme.

ask.q: A carrot is not sour, yet it did not brown. What might the carrot lack?
good: The enzyme.
The chemicals that the enzyme changes.

flow.parent: Banana, apple, potato, brinjal, raw banana, guava and pear usually brown. Tomato, orange, lemon, carrot, cucumber and beetroot usually do not. Sour juice slows the browning enzyme. Other foods, such as carrot, hold very little of the enzyme or of the chemicals it changes. Your family's results are the real answer for your kitchen.
flow.think: A cut fruit is wounded. Why might a plant turn a wound brown?
flow.context: This is day 3 of Who Turns Brown. You sort all the foods you tested and look for a pattern.

challenges.title: Tear-Free Chopping: make the cook's eyes last longer
challenges.problem: In the Onion Sting, a watcher's eyes stung within seconds of the chopping. The family cook has the same problem every day. Your problem is to find a way of chopping that gives the longest time before the first sting. The cook must still be able to see the board and cut safely.
constraints: Use onions of the same kind and about the same size. Use half an onion for each test.
The same person chops every time, in the same way. The same watcher sits 30 centimetres from the board.
The watcher counts the seconds from the first cut to the first sting. Stop at 60 seconds if there is no sting.
Wait five minutes between tests, with a window open, so that eyes and air are fresh.
The cook must be able to see the board clearly and hold the knife safely in every test.
materials: 2 or 3 onions of the same kind
a sharp knife and a board, for the grown-up
a table fan or an open window
anything else your design needs, such as a bowl of water or swimming goggles
general: Chill the onion. Put it in the fridge for an hour, or in the freezer for 15 minutes, before cutting.
Use the sharpest knife in the house, so that fewer cells are crushed.
Put a fan beside the board, or chop next to an open window. Moving air carries the gas away.
creative: Wear swimming goggles, so that the gas cannot reach the eyes.
Peel and halve the onion, and soak the halves in a bowl of water for five minutes before chopping.
Join two methods, such as a chilled onion and a fan together.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own method, or test a family tip such as holding bread in the mouth. Time it against plain chopping. Write the two times, and write whether your method helped.
challenges.context: In this challenge you find a way to chop an onion that gives the longest time before the eyes sting. A grown-up chops, and you time each method.

setup.art: A grown-up chopping half an onion on a board while a child sits a ruler's length away, watching a clock.
setup.caption: 1. First time plain chopping. Count the seconds to the first sting.

setup.art: An onion on a fridge shelf, a table fan beside a chopping board, and a pair of swimming goggles on the counter.
setup.caption: 2. Choose a method: a cold onion, moving air, goggles or your own idea.

setup.art: A notebook page with a list of methods and a number of seconds beside each.
setup.caption: 3. Time each method in the same way. Compare the times.

flow.do: Read the problem together. A grown-up chops half a plain onion from the basket. The watcher counts the seconds from the first cut to the first sting. Write the time down.
flow.say: First we need the time for plain chopping. I will chop, and you count the seconds until your eyes sting. This time is what every method must beat.
flow.kid: Count the seconds until your eyes sting. Write the time down.

ask.q: Why do we time plain chopping before we try any method?
good: We need something to compare with.
Without it we cannot tell whether a method helped.

flow.context: This is the first step of Tear-Free Chopping. You time plain chopping, so that you can compare other methods with it.

flow.do: Your child chooses two or three methods to test and says why each might work. If one method needs a cold onion, put the onion in the freezer now for 15 minutes.
flow.say: The gas is made by enzymes in broken cells, and it reaches your eyes through the air. Choose two or three methods. For each one, say what it does to the gas.
flow.kid: Choose two or three methods. Say why each one might work.
flow.parent: A good reason names what the method changes. Cold slows the enzymes. A sharp knife breaks fewer cells. Moving air or goggles keep the gas from the eyes.
flow.context: In this step of Tear-Free Chopping you choose the methods to test and say why each might work.

flow.do: Test each method on half an onion, with five minutes between tests. The watcher counts the seconds to the first sting each time. Stop at 60 seconds. Write every time down.
flow.say: Now we test each method in the same way. Count the seconds again. I chop in the same way each time, and you sit in the same place.
flow.kid: Time each method. Count the seconds to the first sting.
flow.parent: Results vary with the onion. A chilled onion and a fan each help in most kitchens. If two times are close, repeat both before you decide.
flow.context: In this step of Tear-Free Chopping a grown-up chops with each method and you time the first sting.

flow.do: Compare the times. Then your child changes one thing, or joins two methods, and tests once more.
flow.say: Which method gave the longest time? Change one thing, or join two methods, and test again. Did the method work on the enzymes or on the air?
flow.kid: Which method won? Change one thing. Test again.

ask.q: A whole onion boiled for two minutes and then chopped gives no tears. Why not?
good: Heat destroys the enzymes, so no gas is made.
It is like the boiled apple slice in Hot Dip, Cold Dip, which could not brown.

flow.parent: Praise a clear account of what was tested and what the times showed. A method that did not help is still a result worth writing down.
flow.context: This is the last step of Tear-Free Chopping. You compare the times and improve your best method.

items.p: What three things does a cut apple need in order to turn brown?
opts: Broken cells, an enzyme and oxygen
items.why: Cutting breaks the cells. An enzyme from the cells then joins oxygen from the air to chemicals in the juice. That makes the brown.

items.p: A whole onion is full of tear gas that is waiting to escape.
items.why: False. A whole onion holds no tear gas. The cells make the gas only after a knife breaks them and mixes what was stored apart.

items.p: The stretchy substance that forms when wheat flour is wetted and kneaded is called ____.
a: gluten
items.why: Gluten is a net of wheat proteins. It stretches around gas bubbles and holds them in the dough.

items.p: Match each food to what makes it rise.
items.why: Yeast and bacteria make gas slowly as they feed. Baking soda makes gas at once when it meets a sour food. Steam forms from the water in the dough.

items.p: Sort these. Is each one enzyme browning or heat browning?
items.why: Enzyme browning happens to raw food whose cells are broken, without any heating. Heat browning happens on a hot, dry surface.

items.p: Why does an idli stay white while a dosa turns brown?
opts: Steam is not hot enough to brown
items.why: Steam is at about 100 degrees Celsius, and heat browning needs more. The dry surface of a dosa on a tawa gets far hotter.

items.p: Water in an open pot gets hotter and hotter as it boils.
items.why: False. Boiling water stays at about 100 degrees Celsius. A higher flame only makes it boil away faster.

items.p: Put these steps in order, to show how a chopped onion makes you cry.
items: A stored chemical and an enzyme mix
A gas forms and floats up
Nerve endings on the eye sense the gas
The tear glands send out tears
a: The knife breaks onion cells
A stored chemical and an enzyme mix
A gas forms and floats up
Nerve endings on the eye sense the gas
The tear glands send out tears
items.why: The gas cannot form until the cells are broken. The tears come last, after the nerves have sent their signal to the brain.

items.p: A chemical made by living cells that speeds up one kind of change is called an ____.
a: enzyme
items.why: Each enzyme does one job. One enzyme browns a cut apple, and others make the onion's tear gas.

items.p: What does kneading do to wheat dough?
opts: Links proteins into a stretchy net
items.why: Kneading lines up the wheat proteins and joins them into gluten. The gas is made by yeast, soda or steam, not by kneading.

items.p: An apple slice was held in boiling water for two minutes. It did not turn brown afterwards. Explain why.
items.a: The brown is made by an enzyme from the apple's broken cells. Boiling water destroys the enzyme. With no working enzyme, oxygen is not joined to the chemicals in the juice, so no brown forms.
items.why: A strong answer names the enzyme and says that heat destroyed it. It does not say that the heat cooked the brown away.

items.p: Washed wheat dough leaves a stretchy lump, and washed rice dough leaves nothing. What does this mean for bread?
items.a: The stretchy lump is gluten. Gluten stretches around gas bubbles and holds them, so wheat dough can rise into a loaf. Rice dough has no gluten, so the gas escapes and the dough stays flat.
items.why: A strong answer links the lump to holding gas. It says more than that wheat is stretchy.

items.p: Draw a plant cell with two chemicals stored in separate parts. Then draw the cell after a cut.
items.a: The first drawing shows a cell with two closed bags inside, each holding a different chemical. The second shows the cell cut open, with the two chemicals mixed and a new substance forming.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the chemicals apart before the cut and mixed after it. That mixing is what starts browning and the onion's gas.
items.art: Two empty boxes side by side, labelled 'before the cut' and 'after the cut'.

items.p: Plant breeders have bred onions that make very little tear gas. Should farmers grow them?

views.who: A cook in a hotel kitchen
views.says: I chop a hundred onions a day, and my eyes burn. A tearless onion would make my work easier.
The gas keeps animals off the bulbs. If my onions lose it, more of my crop may be eaten.
The sharp taste comes from the same chemicals as the gas. A tearless onion tastes milder, and some people will miss the bite.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason, using what you know about the onion's gas. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason from the unit. One reason is that the gas is the onion's defence, made only when cells are broken. Another is that chilling or a fan already cuts the tears without changing the onion.
items.why: Each view has something right in it. A strong answer uses a fact about how the gas is made or what it does for the onion.

items.p: Which gas do yeast give off as they feed on sugar?
items.why: Yeast turn sugar into carbon dioxide and a little alcohol. The carbon dioxide makes the bubbles in the dough.

items.p: In Hot Dip, Cold Dip, why was one apple slice dipped in cold water?
opts: To check that wetting was not the cause
items.why: The hot slice was both heated and wetted. The cold slice was only wetted. It still browned, so the heat made the difference.

items.p: In the Tawa Toast Test, the square wet with water stayed pale longest. Why?
opts: It stayed near 100 degrees until dry
It had less bread in it
Water cooled the tawa for good
items.why: Wet bread cannot pass about 100 degrees Celsius until its water has boiled away. Heat browning needs a hotter, dry surface.

items.p: Milk helps bread to brown because milk holds a sugar and proteins.
items.why: True. Heat browning is a reaction between sugars and the building units of proteins. Milk adds both to the surface of the bread.

items.p: Crushed garlic makes tear gas in the same way as a chopped onion.
items.why: False. Garlic has the first enzyme and lacks the second. So crushed garlic makes a strong smell, and no tear gas.

items.p: Sort these gas makers. Is each one alive or not alive?
items.why: Yeast and bacteria are living beings who make gas as they feed. Baking soda, fruit salt and steam make gas by chemistry or by heat.

items.p: Three of these foods are puffed mainly by steam. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: Puri, phulka and popcorn are puffed by water turning to steam. Pav is raised by yeast.

items.p: Steam takes up about 1,600 times as much room as water. How many millilitres of steam do 2 millilitres of water make?
items.why: 2 times 1,600 is 3,200 millilitres. That is more than 3 litres of steam from less than half a teaspoon of water.

items.p: Put these in order, to show what happens to bread dough in a hot oven.
items: The gas bubbles grow as they warm
The yeast die at about 60 degrees Celsius
The walls of the bubbles set firm
a: The gas bubbles grow as they warm
The yeast die at about 60 degrees Celsius
The walls of the bubbles set firm
The crust dries out
The crust turns brown
items.why: The dough swells first, while it is still soft. Then the heat sets it. The crust can brown only after it has dried.

items.p: A cook drops cut potato into a bowl of water. Explain how the water keeps the potato pale.
items.a: Enzyme browning needs oxygen from the air. Under water, very little oxygen reaches the cut surface. So the enzyme cannot make the brown substance.
items.why: A strong answer says that the water keeps oxygen away. It does not say that the water washes the brown off.

items.p: A vada is brown outside and pale inside. Explain why, using the boiling point of water.
items.a: The outside dries in the hot oil and gets much hotter than 100 degrees Celsius, so it browns. The inside is still wet. Wet food stays at about 100 degrees Celsius, which is too low for heat browning.
items.why: A strong answer says that the dry outside can get hotter than the wet inside. It names 100 degrees Celsius as the limit for wet food.

items.p: Many people think browned food is burnt food. What could you show them to prove the difference?
items.a: Toast one piece of bread to golden brown and another until it is black. The golden piece smells good and tastes sweet and nutty. The black piece smells of smoke and tastes bitter. Browning makes new flavours, and burning breaks the food down to carbon.
items.why: A strong answer gives a test or a clear example with two results. It says that browning comes before burning.

items.p: A slice of apple has turned brown on the plate. Is it spoilt?

views.says: Yes. Rotten fruit is brown. I will not eat anything that has changed colour.
No. The apple's own enzyme made the brown in a few minutes. Germs need days to rot a fruit.
It is safe. But nobody buys brown fruit, so shops throw a great deal away.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason, using what you know about enzyme browning. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason from the unit. One reason is that browning starts within minutes and needs only broken cells, an enzyme and air. Another is that the taste and look do change, which matters to people who buy fruit.
items.why: The second child has the science right, and the others raise real points about caution and waste. A strong answer uses a fact about how fast and why the browning happens.

items.p: Label three parts of this loaf cut in half: the crust, a gas hole and the soft inside.
a: The crust: it dried, got hotter than 100 degrees Celsius and browned
A gas hole: a bubble of gas was held here by gluten
The soft inside: it stayed moist and below 100 degrees Celsius, so it stayed pale
items.why: A loaf shows two ideas at once. The holes show where gas was held, and the brown crust shows where the dough dried and got hot.
items.art: A loaf of bread cut in half, showing a brown crust, a pale inside and many small holes, with three empty label lines.

items.p: Which change would make an onion sting less?
items.why: Cold slows the enzymes that make the gas. A blunt knife and fine chopping break more cells, and warmth speeds the enzymes up.

items.p: Mustard seeds popped in hot oil taste nutty and not sharp. Why?
items.why: The sharp substance is made by an enzyme when raw seeds are crushed and wetted. Hot oil destroys the enzyme first, so it is never made.

items.p: Scientists switched off the browning enzyme in apple trees. What happened to the cut apples?
items.why: With no browning enzyme, oxygen is not joined to the chemicals in the juice. These apples were approved for sale in the United States in 2015.

items.p: Onion juice with only the first enzyme made almost no tear gas. What does this show?
opts: The gas is stored in the onion
items.why: If one enzyme were enough, the gas would have formed. Shinsuke Imai's team found the missing second enzyme in 2002.

items.p: In Puff or Flop, a dough has Gas 5 and Hold 2. How many beans does it earn?
items.why: The dough earns the smaller number, 2. It made 5 bubbles of gas but could hold only 2 of them.

items.p: A dough of rice flour alone will rise as high as wheat dough if you add more yeast.
items.why: False. More yeast make more gas, but rice dough has no gluten to hold it. The extra gas escapes.

items.p: Green tea and black tea come from different kinds of bush.
items.why: False. Both come from the same plant. For black tea the rolled leaves brown in the air. For green tea the leaves are heated first, which destroys the enzyme.

items.p: Heating sugar until it turns brown, with no protein, is called ____.
a: caramelising
caramelizing
caramelisation
caramelization
items.why: Table sugar caramelises at about 160 to 170 degrees Celsius. The Maillard reaction is different, because it needs proteins as well as sugars.

items.p: Match each way of keeping cut fruit pale to the reason it works.
items.why: Browning needs broken cells, a working enzyme and oxygen. Each method removes or weakens one of these.

items.p: Put these steps in order, to show how black tea is made.
items: Roll the leaves to break the cells
Leave the leaves in the air to brown
a: Pick the fresh leaves
Let the leaves wilt
Roll the leaves to break the cells
Leave the leaves in the air to brown
Dry the leaves with heat
items.why: The leaves can brown only after rolling has broken their cells. The drying heat comes last, and it stops the browning.

items.p: Plan a fair test: does a cut apple brown more slowly in the fridge? Write what you would change.
items.a: Cut two slices of the same thickness from one apple. Put one on a plate in the fridge and one on a plate on the table. Look at both at the same times and give each a brown score. Only the temperature is different.
items.why: A strong answer changes only the temperature. It keeps the apple, the thickness and the times the same.

items.p: The onion makes tear gas only after cells are broken. How could this timing be useful to the onion?
items.a: The gas is made at the moment an animal bites, and at the place of the bite. The onion does not have to store a stinging gas among their own cells. The gas reaches the eyes and nose of whoever is biting.
items.why: A strong answer links the timing of the gas to a bite. Any sensible reason about defence or about not harming the onion's own cells is good.

items.p: A cake sank in the middle after the oven door was opened too early. Explain what happened inside the cake.
items.a: The walls of the gas bubbles had not yet set firm. Cold air came in, and the warm gas in the bubbles shrank. The soft batter could not hold its shape, so it sank.
items.why: A strong answer says that heat must set the batter before the bubbles can stay. It also says that gas shrinks as it cools.

items.p: Draw a slice through risen wheat dough. Show the gas bubbles and the gluten net around them.
items.a: Many round bubbles of different sizes, each with a thin stretched wall of dough around it. The walls join into one net that runs through the whole slice.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that the gas is inside closed bubbles. The gluten forms the walls, as a balloon skin holds air.
items.art: An empty circle with the heading 'inside risen dough'.

items.p: Dark brown chips and toast hold a little of a chemical called acrylamide. Should a family stop eating browned food?

views.says: Large doses of acrylamide cause cancer in rats and mice. I advise cooking to golden, not dark brown.
Studies of people have not shown clear harm from the small amounts in food. Eating vegetables and playing outside matter far more.
Browning makes the flavour of dosa, toast and roast potato. I fry to golden and scrape off anything black.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason, using what you know about heat browning. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason from the unit. One reason is that browning makes hundreds of new substances, and most give flavour. Another is that food can be cooked to golden, which browns it less.
items.why: Scientists have not settled this, so no view is simply right. A strong answer separates what was found in rats and mice from what is known about people.

items.p: A bread recipe uses boiling water to mix the yeast. What will happen?
opts: The yeast die and make no gas
items.why: Yeast die at about 60 degrees Celsius. Dead yeast cannot feed, so they make no carbon dioxide. Warm water, not hot, suits them best.

items.p: What made the sharp smell in wet, crushed raw mustard?
opts: An enzyme changed a stored chemical
items.why: Crushing and wetting bring a stored chemical and an enzyme together. The enzyme makes the sharp substance within about ten minutes.

quiz.p: Why does a cut brinjal turn brown?
opts: An enzyme uses oxygen from the air
The knife leaves rust on it
quiz.why: Cutting breaks the cells. An enzyme from the cells joins oxygen to chemicals in the juice, and the product is brown. If you chose germs, remember that rotting takes days.

quiz.p: Which of these stops an apple slice from browning?
opts: Leaving it in a sunny place
quiz.why: Boiling water destroys the browning enzyme. Smaller pieces and more air both make browning faster, because more cells are broken and more oxygen arrives.

quiz.p: Lemon juice keeps cut banana pale. Why?
quiz.why: The browning enzyme works badly in sour juice. The vitamin C in lemon also undoes the first step of the browning.

opts: A dry surface hotter than boiling water
quiz.why: Sugars and proteins react fast only above about 140 degrees Celsius. A wet surface stays near 100 degrees Celsius, so it must dry first.

quiz.p: Boiled rice never browns in the pot. Why?
opts: Boiling water stays at about 100 degrees
Rice has no sugar or protein
The lid keeps the air out
quiz.why: Rice has both starch and protein, and it browns well when fried. In boiling water it cannot get hot enough.

quiz.p: Which food is puffed by steam alone?
quiz.why: A puri has no yeast and no soda. Water in the dough turns to steam in the hot oil. Pav uses yeast, dhokla uses soda, and idli batter is fermented.

quiz.p: What do yeast need in order to make gas?
quiz.why: Yeast are living beings. They feed on sugar in warm, wet dough and give off carbon dioxide. Cold slows them, and great heat kills them.

quiz.p: Why can wheat dough hold gas bubbles?
opts: It is heavier than rice dough
quiz.why: Gluten is a stretchy net of wheat proteins. It stretches around each bubble. Starch washes away in water and does not stretch.

quiz.p: What is left when a ball of wheat dough is washed in water?
quiz.why: The starch floats away and turns the water white. The gluten stays in the hand. If you chose nothing, that is what rice dough leaves.

quiz.p: Where is the tear gas before an onion is cut?
opts: It has not been made yet
In the middle of the bulb
quiz.why: A whole onion holds the makings of the gas in separate parts of each cell. The gas forms only after a cut mixes them.

quiz.p: Why does a chilled onion sting less?
quiz.why: Enzymes work more slowly when they are cold, so less gas is made in the first minute. The gas also rises more slowly from a cold onion.

quiz.p: In a fair test of three apple slices, what should be different?
opts: Only the dip each slice gets
The apple each slice came from
The time you look at each
quiz.why: A fair test changes one thing and keeps the rest the same. Then any difference in browning must come from the dip.

applications: Tea factories in Assam, Darjeeling, the Nilgiris and Munnar roll tea leaves and let them brown to make black tea. They heat the leaves first to make green tea.
Factories that freeze peas, beans and sweetcorn dip them in boiling water first. This destroys the enzymes, so the vegetables keep their colour for months.
Makers of fruit juice add vitamin C, so that apple and guava juice do not turn brown in the packet.
Bakers choose flour by its gluten. Flour with more gluten makes tall loaves of bread, and flour with less makes soft cakes and biscuits.
Coffee roasters heat green coffee beans until they turn brown. The roasting makes the smell of coffee by heat browning.
Plant breeders have bred onions that make very little tear gas, and apples whose slices stay pale.

open_questions.q: Which substances give browned food its smell and taste?
open_questions.why_open: The Maillard reaction makes hundreds of substances in one piece of toast. Chemists have named many of them, but nobody has a full list for any food.

open_questions.q: Does the acrylamide in dark brown food harm people?
open_questions.why_open: Large doses cause cancer in rats and mice. Studies of people who eat ordinary amounts have not given a clear answer.

open_questions.q: What does the browning enzyme do for a plant?
open_questions.why_open: It may protect wounds from microbes and insects, and it may have other jobs in the cell. Plants with the enzyme switched off still grow, so its use is not settled.

open_questions.q: Did cooking change the bodies and brains of our ancestors?
open_questions.why_open: The scientist Richard Wrangham argues that cooked food gave early humans more energy. Nobody yet knows how early our ancestors controlled fire, so the idea is debated.

open_questions.q: Can a dough without gluten hold gas as well as wheat dough does?
open_questions.why_open: Food scientists mix gums, starches and other proteins to copy gluten. No mixture yet stretches and holds gas quite as well.
