maths.problem: In Hot Dip, Cold Dip, three apple slices were scored after 40 minutes. The scores were 3 for no dip, 2 for the cold dip and 0 for the hot dip. Which dip made the bigger difference? What does the cold-dip score tell you about wetting?
maths.answer: The hot dip made the bigger difference. It lowered the score by 3, and the cold dip lowered it by only 1. So wetting alone does very little.
maths.explain: 3 take away 0 is 3 for the hot dip. 3 take away 2 is 1 for the cold dip. Both slices were wet, so the extra 2 points must come from the heat.
maths.context: In Hot Dip, Cold Dip you dip apple slices in cold water and in boiling water. Then you score how brown they turn. These are made-up scores from 0 to 3.
maths.why_maths: Taking one score from another shows how much of the change came from the heat.

maths.problem: In Tear-Free Chopping, plain chopping stung after 15 seconds. With a fan it took 45 seconds, and with a chilled onion 30 seconds. A chilled onion with a fan reached 60 seconds, when the test stopped. How many times as long as plain chopping did the fan and the chilled onion last? Why can the last result not be compared fairly?
maths.answer: The fan lasted 3 times as long, and the chilled onion 2 times as long. The last test was stopped at 60 seconds, so its real time is unknown.
maths.explain: 45 divided by 15 is 3. 30 divided by 15 is 2. The chilled onion with the fan lasted at least 4 times as long, because 60 divided by 15 is 4. It might have lasted much longer.
maths.context: In Tear-Free Chopping a grown-up chops onions in different ways, and you count the seconds until your eyes sting. These are made-up times.
maths.why_maths: Dividing by the plain time shows how much each method helped. It also shows what a test that was stopped early cannot tell you.

maths.problem: In Wash the Dough, 60 grams of maida left a lump of gluten that weighed 15 grams. What fraction of the flour's weight is that? How heavy a lump would 240 grams of the same flour leave?
maths.answer: One quarter. 240 grams of flour would leave about 60 grams.
maths.explain: 15 out of 60 is the same as 1 out of 4. One quarter of 240 is 60. The lump is wet, so part of its weight is water.
maths.context: In Wash the Dough you wash a ball of wheat dough until only a stretchy lump of gluten is left. These are made-up weights from a kitchen scale.
maths.why_maths: A fraction lets you work out how much gluten any amount of the same flour would give.

maths.problem: 1 millilitre of water makes about 1,600 millilitres of steam. A drop of water is about one twentieth of a millilitre. A puffed puri holds about 80 millilitres. Is one drop of water enough to fill the puri with steam?
maths.answer: Yes. One drop makes about 80 millilitres of steam, which just fills the puri.
maths.explain: One twentieth of 1,600 is 1,600 divided by 20, which is 80. A puri's dough holds far more than one drop of water, so there is steam to spare.
maths.context: In Puff or Flop, a card says that hot oil turns the water in puri dough to steam. Steam takes up about 1,600 times as much room as the water it came from.
maths.why_maths: Dividing shows how little water is needed to blow a thin disc of dough up into a ball.

maths.problem: In Two Katori Dhoklas, both batters were 2 centimetres deep. After steaming, the one with fruit salt was 3.6 centimetres high and the plain one was 2.2 centimetres. How much did each one rise? How many times as much did the first one rise?
maths.answer: The one with fruit salt rose 1.6 centimetres, and the plain one rose 0.2 centimetres. The first rose 8 times as much.
maths.explain: 3.6 take away 2 is 1.6. 2.2 take away 2 is 0.2. Eight lots of 0.2 make 1.6. The plain batter still rose a little, because air and steam swell in the heat.
maths.context: In Two Katori Dhoklas you steam one katori of batter with fruit salt and one without, and measure both. These are made-up heights.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the two rises shows how much of the rising came from the fruit salt.

maths.problem: In Puff or Flop, a dough has Gas 6 and Hold 2. One card adds 3 to Gas. Another card adds 3 to Hold. Which card gives more beans, and how many more?
maths.answer: The Hold card. It gives 5 beans, and the Gas card gives only 2. That is 3 more.
maths.explain: The rise is the smaller of the two numbers. With the Gas card the numbers are 9 and 2, so the rise is 2. With the Hold card they are 6 and 5, so the rise is 5.
maths.context: In Puff or Flop you roll a die for the gas a dough makes. You roll again for the gas it can hold. You take beans equal to the smaller number.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the two numbers shows which one is holding the dough back. Only raising that number helps.

quiz: A whole onion is full of tear gas.
The onion's cells make the gas only after they are cut.
A cut apple needs oxygen in order to turn brown.
An enzyme joins oxygen from the air to chemicals in the juice.
Boiling water makes an apple slice brown faster.
Boiling water destroys the browning enzyme, so the slice stays pale.
Wet food cannot get much hotter than 100 degrees Celsius.
The water in it boils at about 100 degrees Celsius and gets no hotter.
Toast turns brown because of an enzyme in the bread.
Toast browns because heat makes sugars and proteins react.
Yeast are living beings.
Yeast are fungi of one cell each, who feed on sugar and make gas.
A puri is puffed up by yeast.
A puri is puffed by steam from the water in the dough.
Rice flour dough holds gas as well as wheat dough.
Rice flour forms no gluten, so the gas escapes.
Gluten is the part of wheat dough that stretches.
Gluten is a net of wheat proteins that stretches around gas bubbles.
A chilled onion makes fewer tears.
Cold slows the enzymes that make the tear gas.
odd: The apple, banana and brinjal brown by an enzyme, but toast browns by heat.
Yeast, baking soda and steam make gas, but gluten holds the gas.
Idli, rice and dhokla cook in steam or water and stay pale, but a dosa browns on a hot tawa.
Chilling, a sharp knife and a fan all make fewer tears, but a blunt knife crushes more cells.
Rice, ragi and jowar form no gluten, but wheat does.

how_we_found_out.story: By the 1970s chemists knew what the onion's tear gas was. They also knew that an onion holds an enzyme called alliinase, which starts work when cells are broken. For about thirty years, books said that this one enzyme did the whole job. The gas was thought to form by itself from what the enzyme made. In Japan, Shinsuke Imai and his team at a food company were studying onions and garlic. They mixed the onion's stored chemical with alliinase. Almost no tear gas formed. Then they added another part of the onion's juice, and the gas appeared. So the juice held a second enzyme that nobody had known about. They found it, and they described it in the journal Nature in 2002. Garlic lacks this second enzyme, which is why garlic does not make us cry. In 2008 Colin Eady's team in New Zealand switched off the second enzyme in onion plants. Those onions made almost no tear gas.
how_we_found_out.who: Shinsuke Imai and his team at House Foods in Japan, and Colin Eady and his team in New Zealand
how_we_found_out.when: The tear gas was identified in the early 1970s. Imai's team reported the second enzyme in 2002. Eady's team reported onions without it in 2008.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That one enzyme, alliinase, makes the onion's tear gas, and that the gas then forms by itself. Imai's team showed that alliinase alone made almost no gas, and that a second enzyme is needed.

roots.context: In this unit you found that an onion's sting and an apple's brown are made after the cut. Here we ask what a thing holds before it is cut, and what that tells us about living beings.

deep_truth.truth: In the Onion Sting, a whole onion near your eyes did nothing, and a chopped onion stung. A whole onion holds no tear gas. Each cell stores two chemicals in separate parts, and a knife makes them meet. So the sting is made after the cut, by the onion's own cells.
deep_truth.habit: We speak as if the sting, the smell and the colour of a food are stored inside it. Some of them do not exist until the cells are broken. What the plant holds is the means to make them.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Onion Sting, the whole onion did not sting, and the chopped onion stung within seconds. In Wake the Mustard, the dry crushed seeds were mild, and the wet raw paste turned sharp in ten minutes. In Hot Dip, Cold Dip, the boiled slice could not turn brown. So the brown is made by something that heat destroys.

three.who_am_i: Your skin makes its brown colour with an enzyme closely related to the one that browns a cut apple. You and an apple share some of the same tools.
three.what_is_life: An onion bulb is alive. They keep two chemicals apart in every cell, ready for the moment an animal bites. Plants sense wounds and answer them.
three.what_is_this_world: An idli and a dosa are made from much the same batter. What the batter becomes depends on heat, water and time. The same matter can become many things.

roots.thread: A whole onion, a whole apple and a dry mustard seed look finished. Yet each one holds chemicals that have not met. When they meet, something appears that was not there before: a gas, a colour or a sharp taste. Many sages taught that the many things of the world come from one source, which holds them all as possibilities. The science here says something smaller and plain. What a thing can become is part of what that thing is.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka asks his son Shvetaketu to split the fruit of a banyan, and then one of its tiny seeds. The boy sees nothing inside. His father says that the great tree grows from that fineness, which he cannot see.
teachings.link: You cannot find the tear gas in a whole onion, because it is not there yet. The onion holds the means to make it, as the seed holds the means to make a tree. The Upanishad uses the seed to point to the self, which science does not test.

teachings.source: Udana 1.1, a saying of the Buddha
teachings.teaching: When this is, that comes to be. When this arises, that arises.
teachings.link: The sting arises only when broken cells, two enzymes, moving air and an eye come together. Take one away, and there are no tears. That is how you beat the sting in Tear-Free Chopping.

teachings.source: Jagadish Chandra Bose, Response in the Living and Non-Living (1902)
teachings.teaching: Bose recorded electrical signals in plants. He showed that a plant answers a touch or a blow with a signal, as an animal's muscle does.
teachings.link: A cut onion answers the knife with chemistry. Bose showed that plants also answer with electricity. He went further and said that metals respond in the same way, and most scientists do not accept that part.

science.text: When a caterpillar bites one leaf of a thale cress plant, a signal reaches the plant's other leaves within minutes. Those leaves then begin to make defence chemicals.
The enzyme that browns a cut apple belongs to a family of enzymes. Another enzyme of that family makes melanin, the brown colour of human skin.
Whether a plant feels a wound in a way that is like an animal's pain is not known.

other_view.view: The onion's gas is simply what forms when two chemicals meet, as baking soda fizzes when it meets lemon juice. Nothing is chosen at the moment of the cut. Long ago, onions who happened to store these chemicals were eaten less often. So more of them lived to make seeds. On this view, 'defence' is a handy word for that result. It tells us nothing about what an onion senses.

practice.title: One leaf, two breaths
practice.say: Take one curry leaf, or a leaf of mint, tulsi or coriander. Hold the whole leaf under your nose and breathe in slowly, twice. Now tear the leaf in half and rub it once between your fingers. Breathe in slowly, twice more. The smell reached you when the cells were broken. Sit quietly for five breaths, and notice how long the smell stays.
practice.kid: Hold a whole leaf under your nose. Breathe in twice. Tear the leaf. Breathe in twice more. Sit quietly for five breaths.

ask: In the Onion Sting, the whole onion did not sting and the chopped onion did. Where was the sting before the knife came?
The onion makes the gas when an animal bites. People cut onions anyway, and then plant more of them. What has the onion gained?
Your skin and a cut apple make brown colour with related enzymes. What else might you share with an apple?

playtest: Read through as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, step by step. The experiments were reasoned through carefully, but they have not yet been tried at home. The Onion Sting (core) needs one onion and a grown-up with a knife. A whole onion does not sting, and chopping usually stings within 10 to 40 seconds from a ruler's length away. Mild onions take longer, and a parent can be the watcher if the child prefers. Hot Dip, Cold Dip (core) needs one apple and a small pan of boiling water. A plain slice usually browns clearly within 40 minutes, and a slice boiled for two minutes stays pale. Some kinds of apple brown slowly. The last step says to repeat with a banana or a brinjal if so. The Tawa Toast Test (core) needs one slice of bread, sugar, milk and a tawa. The water square usually stays palest, and the sugar and milk squares end darkest. The order of the dry square and the milk square can vary with the flame. The sugar square can burn quickly, so the flame must stay low. Wash the Dough (core) works best with maida. Atta gives a smaller lump with specks of bran. The washing is messy and takes about 15 minutes. The lump breaks into shreds if it is squeezed hard at the start. Two Katori Dhoklas needs fruit salt or baking soda. The batter must go into the steam within a minute of adding it. Wake the Mustard uses brown or black mustard seeds. The seeds must be roasted under a lid, because they jump. Tear-Free Chopping gives results that vary from onion to onion, so close times should be repeated. Who Turns Brown uses only pieces of food that are being cut for meals. No part needs a garden.
